docs.title: KeyLease
docs.text:
A Soroban protocol on Stellar that turns metered API/RPC access into time-bound, escrowed micro-leases.

KeyLease replaces long-lived static API keys with leases: expiring on-chain authorizations backed by a SEP-41 micropayment held in Soroban escrow. Providers publish a price instead of a secret; consumers pay only for the calls they use; the Stellar ledger holds the truth about every lease.

  • Repository: keylease-core — the Soroban contracts
  • License: MIT

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: KeyLease is one Soroban contract and the Stellar ledger it runs on. There is no second source of truth: services, leases, escrow balances and lifecycle history all live on-chain, and the contract exposes them through entry points and contract events.

docs.title: KeyLeaseRegistry
docs.text:
A pure Rust Soroban contract. It is the only component that can move value.

Module Role lib.rs Entry points, contractmeta!, upgrade, lifecycle documentation. types.rs Service, Lease, LeaseStatus. storage.rs DataKey layout, instance/persistent split, duration-aware TTL policy. events.rs Typed #[contractevent] payloads for every transition. errors.rs Stable error codes (part of the ABI).

The registry is deliberately small. It does not know what an HTTP request is, what the endpoint does, or who is calling it. It knows service_id, allocated_calls, expires_at and locked_deposit.

docs.title: SEP-41 token
docs.text:
The registry holds no privileged token logic. It calls the standard SEP-41 transfer on the token configured by the admin:

  • the native Stellar Asset Contract wraps XLM (the usual Testnet choice),
  • any custom SEP-41 asset works without a contract change,
  • contracts/mock_token exists only for tests and local sandboxes.

The token boundary is a cross-contract call, so the money paths follow checks-effects-interactions and are tested against a re-entrant token.

docs.title: Consumers of the ledger
docs.text:
There is no privileged off-chain service. Anyone can observe the protocol using standard Stellar tooling:

Consumer How it reads the protocol Provider request path get_lease over Soroban RPC (cached for a short TTL), or a local projection built from the event stream. Accounting / dashboards stellar events, Horizon or an indexer subscribing to lease_created / lease_settled / lease_revoked. CLI tooling stellar contract invoke for writes and reads (reads need any funded --source-account).

See Integration for the concrete verification pipeline.

docs.title: Data flow: one metered call
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Consumer
    participant R as KeyLeaseRegistry
    participant T as SEP-41 token
    participant P as Provider service
    participant U as Upstream API

    C->>R: create_lease(consumer, service_id, calls, duration)
    R->>T: transfer(consumer → registry, rate × calls)
    R-->>C: lease_id + lease_created event
    C->>P: request + Stellar-signed proof of consumer address
    P->>R: get_lease(lease_id)   (TTL-cached)
    R-->>P: Lease { allocated_calls, used_calls, expires_at, settled, ... }
    alt lease active, unexpired, quota remains
        P->>U: forwarded request
        U-->>P: response
        P-->>C: response + x-keylease-calls-remaining
    else invalid / expired / quota exhausted
        P-->>C: 401 / 403 / 429
    end
    P->>R: settle_lease(provider, lease_id, verified_calls)
    R->>T: payout + refund
    R-->>P: lease_settled event

docs.title: Why the contract is minimal
docs.text:
Every line of on-chain code is attack surface for escrowed funds. endpoint_hash is a commitment precisely so the contract never has to reason about off-chain credentials. Usage reporting is a single settlement call rather than one transaction per API call, which keeps the protocol affordable for small allotments.

Off-chain enforcement is replaceable. A provider can read leases directly over RPC, run an indexer, or write their own middleware. The protocol does not depend on any of those being alive: if a proxy is down, providers can still settle with stellar contract invoke, and consumers can still revoke.

Trust flows one way. Off-chain code trusts the ledger for lease state. The contract trusts nobody: every mutating entry point authenticates the actor it claims to represent, and the consumer always has an exit.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: Key Storage TTL policy Admin, Token instance extended on every state change (≈30 days) ServiceCount, LeaseCount instance same as instance Service(u64) persistent extended on save and by bump_service (≈30 days) Lease(u64) persistent extended for the lease's remaining term plus the 24h grace window and a one-day read buffer, or by bump_lease

docs.title: What extends a TTL, and what does not
docs.text:
An extension moves the entry's liveUntilLedgerSeq, which the host books as a rent bump and bills the caller for across the whole extended horizon. Only these calls extend anything: init, set_token, upgrade, register_service, set_service_active, create_lease, settle_lease, revoke_expired_lease, bump_service and bump_lease — and, since PR #152, set_token only when it actually changes the configured token. Every read-only view — get_service, get_lease, lease_status, remaining_calls, locked_balance — is pure, so a simulation of a view costs instructions and no rent. At the ledger where an extension is due, get_lease estimates at 113 stroops (all instructions) against 48,798 for bump_lease, of which 48,684 is persistent rent.

Because reads stopped bumping, state that is only ever looked at has to be kept alive deliberately, and create_lease therefore extends the service it leases from: an actively leased service never goes stale under its own leases.

create_lease caps duration_secs at MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS (30 days), so the TTL extension is bounded and a locked deposit can never outlive its entry. Only the time a lease can be acted on is paid for, so Soroban rent does not dominate short leases.

Three bounds sit on top of each other, and each one is deliberately below the next:

Bound Ledgers Set by longest lease's policy ask (30-day term + 24h grace + 1-day buffer) 552,960 MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS contract ceiling for any single extension 1,555,200 (90 days) MAX_ENTRY_TTL_LEDGERS network maxEntryTtl 6,312,000 Stellar protocol

The ceiling is above every horizon a valid lease can produce, so it never truncates one; what it bounds is an entry whose expires_at was not produced by today's create_lease — one migrated in by an upgrade, or one created after the duration cap is raised. Each extension also takes the minimum of that ceiling and env.storage().max_ttl(), so a network that lowers maxEntryTtl is followed rather than contradicted.

docs.title: Consumer guide
docs.text: You want metered access to an API or RPC endpoint without a permanent static key. This guide walks through buying, using and reclaiming a lease with Stellar.

docs.title: The deal you are getting
docs.text:
• You prepay rate_per_call × requested_calls into Soroban escrow.
  • You get an on-chain authorization that expires after duration_secs.
  • You pay only for the calls you use: unused balance is refunded at settlement.
  • If the provider never settles, you reclaim the entire deposit 24 hours after expiry — no support ticket, no trust required.

Your Stellar account is your identity. There is no API key to copy into a .env file and no separate credential service.

docs.title: 1. Pick a service
docs.text:
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account <funded-account> \
  --network testnet -- get_service --service_id 1

Returns the provider, rate_per_call, is_active and endpoint_hash. Confirm the endpoint_hash matches the endpoint descriptor the provider published off-chain before you escrow anything.

docs.title: 2. Fund your account
docs.text:
Any SEP-41 token the registry is configured with can be escrowed. On Testnet the native asset's SAC is the usual choice, and Friendbot funds accounts with 10,000 fake XLM.

# Testnet only: create + fund in one step
stellar keys generate consumer --network testnet --fund

# or fund an address you already have
curl "https://friendbot.stellar.org?addr=$(stellar keys address consumer)"

docs.title: 3. Create the lease
docs.text:
export REGISTRY=<your registry contract id>
export CONSUMER=$(stellar keys address consumer)

stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- create_lease \
     --consumer $CONSUMER \
     --service_id 1 \
     --requested_calls 500 \
     --duration_secs 3600

This escrows rate_per_call × 500 and prints the new lease_id. The transaction emits lease_created { lease_id, service_id, consumer, allocated_calls, expires_at, locked_deposit, rate_per_call }; keep the transaction hash as proof of purchase.

Choose your numbers deliberately. If your lease expires while you still have unused calls, those calls are not usable — remaining_calls drops to 0 at expires_at. The maximum duration is 30 days (MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS). Under-buy with a generous duration, then renew, rather than over-buying with a short one.

rate_per_call × requested_calls also has a ceiling: MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT (1,000,000,000,000 base units, so 100,000 of a seven-decimal token). A lease above it reverts with DepositTooLarge before the token is called, so an over-typed call count cannot escrow the wrong amount even when your balance would cover it.

Order of arguments matters. consumer is the first argument. This is the exact ABI; older documentation that shows service first is wrong.

docs.title: 4. Use the access
docs.text:
Tell the provider which lease backs your requests. Because the lease records your Stellar address, the provider authenticates you with a Stellar signature (SEP-10 challenge–response, or an equivalent signed challenge) and checks that you are lease.consumer. No bearer token is issued by KeyLease, and none is needed.

Concretely, for a provider that follows Integration:

  1. complete the provider's Stellar challenge with your account,
  2. send requests with your lease_id (path, query or header, as the provider documents) or let the provider resolve it from your authenticated address,
  3. read x-keylease-calls-remaining if the provider exposes it.

If you can sign for the account that owns the lease, you can use it — there is no separate credential to store or rotate. If you rotate that account, create a new lease from the new one.

docs.title: 5. Watch the lease
docs.text:
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- get_lease --lease_id 1

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- remaining_calls --lease_id 1

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- lease_status --lease_id 1

lease_status is 0 (Active), 1 (Expired) or 2 (Settled).

docs.title: 6. Get your money back
docs.text:
Normal path — automatic. When the provider settles, the unused balance is transferred back to you in the same transaction. Nothing to claim.

Provider went dark. After expires_at + 24 hours, reclaim everything:

stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- revoke_expired_lease --consumer $CONSUMER --lease_id 1

This refunds the full locked_deposit and emits lease_revoked { lease_id, consumer, refund }. It works for a lease that was never used and for one that was partially used but never settled.

docs.title: Why you must wait 24 hours
docs.text: That window is reserved for the provider to settle legitimately. It is the provider's guarantee, and your refund is the counterweight. It is a fixed constant in the contract (SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS = 86_400).

docs.title: Refund decision table
docs.text: Lease state What happens Provider settles before/at expiry You get locked_deposit − used × rate back Provider settles after expiry within 24h Same as above Provider settles with verified_calls = 0 You get the entire deposit back Provider never settles, now ≥ expiry + 24h You revoke and get the entire deposit Provider never settles, inside the 24h window Nothing yet — wait

docs.title: Costs
docs.text:
Creating a lease and revoking one are two Soroban transactions (network fees plus the escrow transfer). There is no per-call on-chain cost — the provider settles with a single call count. Check the current fee with stellar network settings or your RPC provider.

create_lease also pays storage rent for keeping the lease entry alive through its term, the 24-hour grace window and a one-day buffer. Rent depends on duration, not call count, so a short lease with a larger allotment is cheaper per call than a long lease with a tiny one. The network enforces a minimum persistent TTL (≈7 days on Testnet), so a very short lease still pays that floor.

docs.title: Contract reference
docs.text:
KeyLeaseRegistry — the Soroban escrow and accounting contract for KeyLease. This page is generated by hand from contracts/registry/src/; treat the source as authoritative.

  • Package: keylease-registry
  • Wasm: target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm
  • Network target: Stellar (wasm32v1-none), soroban-sdk 26
  • Constants: SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS = 86_400 (24 hours), MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS = 2_592_000 (30 days), MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT = 1_000_000_000_000 base units (100,000 of a seven-decimal token such as XLM)
  • Storage TTL: LEDGER_BUMP_THRESHOLD = 17_280, LEDGER_BUMP_EXTEND = 518_400, MAX_ENTRY_TTL_LEDGERS = 1_555_200 (90 days); leases extend to term + 24h grace + a 1-day buffer, clamped to MAX_ENTRY_TTL_LEDGERS and to the network's live maxEntryTtl. Only writes and the two bump_* entry points extend a TTL; reads never do.
  • On-chain metadata: name = KeyLeaseRegistry, version, eventSchemaVersion, description, repository, embedded with contractmeta!

Every state-changing entry point calls require_auth() on the actor it represents. Errors are returned as Result<_, Error>; codes are stable and never renumbered. Every money-moving path persists its effect before calling the SEP-41 token (checks-effects-interactions).

docs.title: init
docs.text:
pub fn init(env: Env, admin: Address) -> Result<(), Error>

Initialize the registry and appoint admin.

  • Caller / auth: admin must authorize.
  • Trigger: once, immediately after deploy.
  • Preconditions: the registry must not already be initialized.
  • State: sets Admin; extends instance TTL.
  • Events: registry_initialized { admin }.
  • Errors: AlreadyInitialized.
  • Notes: the admin can only call set_token and manage upgrades through the propose/execute/cancel flow below. It cannot move user funds.

docs.title: set_token
docs.text:
pub fn set_token(env: Env, admin: Address, token: Address) -> Result<(), Error>

Point the registry at the SEP-41 token used for every deposit and payout.

  • Caller / auth: admin, and admin must match the stored admin.
  • Trigger: once at setup; again only to migrate the escrow asset.
  • State: sets Token; extends instance TTL.
  • Events: escrow_token_set { admin, token } — only when the token actually changes.
  • Errors: NotInitialized, Unauthorized.
  • Notes: the native Stellar Asset Contract (SAC) is the usual value. Changing the token while leases are unsettled is a migration hazard — settle first.
  • Idempotent: calling set_token with the token that is already configured returns Ok(()) and does nothing — no storage write, no TTL extension and no event — so a repeated call cannot be mistaken for a migration. Auth and the stored-admin check still run first, so an unauthorized caller receives Unauthorized either way.

docs.title: propose_upgrade
docs.text:
pub fn propose_upgrade(
    env: Env,
    admin: Address,
    new_wasm_hash: BytesN<32>,
) -> Result<(), Error>

Queue a Wasm upgrade behind the mandatory UPGRADE_DELAY_SECS (24h) delay.

  • Caller / auth: admin, and admin must match the stored admin.
  • Trigger: a released bug fix or feature, after uploading the Wasm with stellar contract upload.
  • State: writes PendingUpgrade { new_wasm_hash, execute_after }; a new proposal replaces the old one and restarts the delay.
  • Events: upgrade_proposed { schema_version, admin, new_wasm_hash, execute_after }.
  • Errors: NotInitialized, Unauthorized, Overflow.
  • Notes: execute_after is a ledger timestamp. Consumers can read it with get_pending_upgrade and exit before it is reached.

docs.title: cancel_upgrade
docs.text:
pub fn cancel_upgrade(env: Env, admin: Address) -> Result<(), Error>

Drop a pending proposal without installing any code.

  • Caller / auth: admin, and admin must match the stored admin.
  • Effects: removes PendingUpgrade.
  • Events: upgrade_cancelled { schema_version, admin, new_wasm_hash }.
  • Errors: NotInitialized, Unauthorized, NoPendingUpgrade.

docs.title: execute_upgrade
docs.text:
pub fn execute_upgrade(env: Env, admin: Address) -> Result<(), Error>

Install the proposed Wasm through env.deployer().update_current_contract_wasm.

  • Caller / auth: admin, and admin must match the stored admin.
  • Preconditions: a proposal exists and ledger.timestamp() >= execute_after.
  • Effects: removes PendingUpgrade and installs the proposed hash.
  • Events: contract_upgraded { schema_version, admin, new_wasm_hash, execute_after }.
  • Errors: NotInitialized, Unauthorized, NoPendingUpgrade, UpgradeDelayNotElapsed.
  • Notes: the contract id, storage and balances are preserved, so an upgrade must never change the DataKey layout or the meaning of stored values. See Deployment.

docs.title: register_service
docs.text:
pub fn register_service(
    env: Env,
    provider: Address,
    rate_per_call: i128,
    endpoint_hash: BytesN<32>,
) -> Result<u64, Error>

Publish a new leasable service.

  • Caller / auth: provider must authorize.
  • Trigger: when a provider lists an API or RPC endpoint.
  • Parameters:
  • rate_per_call — price per metered call in token stroops; must be > 0.
  • endpoint_hash — 32-byte commitment to the off-chain descriptor.
  • Returns: the new service_id (monotonic, starts at 1).
  • State: writes Service(service_id), increments ServiceCount, extends instance TTL.
  • Events: service_registered { service_id, provider, rate_per_call, endpoint_hash }.
  • Errors: InvalidRate, Overflow.

docs.title: set_service_active
docs.text:
pub fn set_service_active(
    env: Env,
    provider: Address,
    service_id: u64,
    is_active: bool,
) -> Result<(), Error>

Pause or resume new leases for a service.

  • Caller / auth: provider, and it must own the service.
  • Trigger: maintenance, incident response, or retirement.
  • State: updates Service(service_id).is_active.
  • Events: service_status_changed { service_id, provider, is_active }.
  • Errors: ServiceNotFound, Unauthorized.
  • Notes: existing leases stay valid and settleable. Deactivation only blocks create_lease.

docs.title: create_lease
docs.text:
pub fn create_lease(
    env: Env,
    consumer: Address,
    service_id: u64,
    requested_calls: u32,
    duration_secs: u64,
) -> Result<u64, Error>

Lock a deposit and mint a time-bound lease.

  • Caller / auth: consumer must authorize.
  • Trigger: a developer purchases metered access.
  • Preconditions: requested_calls > 0, 0 < duration_secs ≤ MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS, rate_per_call × requested_calls ≤ MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT, the service exists and is_active, and Token is set.
  • Effects: transfer(consumer → contract, rate_per_call × requested_calls).
  • Returns: the new lease_id (monotonic, starts at 1).
  • State: writes Lease(lease_id) with expires_at = ledger.timestamp() + duration_secs and a TTL covering the term plus grace; increments LeaseCount.
  • Events: lease_created { lease_id, service_id, consumer, allocated_calls, expires_at, locked_deposit, rate_per_call }. rate_per_call is a snapshot taken at creation, so indexers can interpret locked_deposit without reading the service at the event's ledger.
  • Errors: InvalidCalls, InvalidDuration, DurationTooLong, ServiceNotFound, ServiceInactive, InvalidRate, TokenNotSet, Overflow, DepositTooLarge.

The deposit is bounded twice, and the two rejections mean different things. Overflow says rate_per_call × requested_calls does not fit i128. DepositTooLarge says it fits and is still more than one lease may lock. The bound is checked after the multiplication and before the lease id is allocated or the token is called, so a rejected lease moves nothing and consumes no id.

docs.title: settle_lease
docs.text:
pub fn settle_lease(
    env: Env,
    provider: Address,
    lease_id: u64,
    verified_calls: u32,
) -> Result<(), Error>

Pay the provider for verified calls and refund the remainder to the consumer.

  • Caller / auth: provider, and it must own the lease's service.
  • Trigger: at or after expiry, or as soon as every allocated call is consumed.
  • Preconditions: lease exists, is not settled, verified_calls ≤ allocated_calls, the caller owns the service, and the lease has expired or verified_calls == allocated_calls.
  • Effects: persists used_calls and settled = true first, then calls transfer(contract → provider, verified_calls × rate_per_call) and transfer(contract → consumer, locked_deposit − payout).
  • Events: lease_settled { lease_id, provider, verified_calls, payout, refund }.
  • Errors: LeaseNotFound, LeaseAlreadySettled, InvalidCalls, Unauthorized, LeaseNotSettleable, TokenNotSet, Overflow.
  • Notes: zero-value transfers are skipped. Settling with verified_calls = 0 is a legitimate way for a provider to refund an unusable lease. A re-entrant token sees settled = true and is rejected.

docs.title: revoke_expired_lease
docs.text:
pub fn revoke_expired_lease(
    env: Env,
    consumer: Address,
    lease_id: u64,
) -> Result<(), Error>

Reclaim the full deposit when the provider never settled.

  • Caller / auth: consumer, and it must be the lease's consumer.
  • Trigger: after expires_at + SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS.
  • Effects: persists settled = true first, then transfer(contract → consumer, locked_deposit).
  • Events: lease_revoked { lease_id, consumer, refund }.
  • Errors: LeaseNotFound, Unauthorized, LeaseAlreadySettled, LeaseNotExpired, RevokeWindowNotElapsed, TokenNotSet, Overflow.
  • Notes: this is the consumer's escape hatch, and the reason escrow is safe against an unresponsive provider.

docs.title: Storage maintenance
docs.text: Reads no longer keep entries alive, so extending a lifetime is an explicit, metered call of its own. Both entry points are permissionless: the caller pays for the extension with their own transaction fee, and the horizon comes from the contract's policy rather than from the caller.

docs.title: bump_service
docs.text:
pub fn bump_service(env: Env, service_id: u64) -> Result<(), Error>

Extend a service entry to LEDGER_BUMP_EXTEND ledgers.

  • Caller / auth: anyone.
  • Errors: ServiceNotFound — a miss is an error, not a silent no-op, so a caller never pays for an extension that kept nothing alive.
  • Notes: create_lease extends the service it leases from, so an actively used service does not need this. It exists for a published-but-idle service.

docs.title: bump_lease
docs.text:
pub fn bump_lease(env: Env, lease_id: u64) -> Result<(), Error>

Extend a lease entry using the lease TTL policy (remaining term + 24h grace + a 1-day buffer, clamped to MAX_ENTRY_TTL_LEDGERS and the network's maxEntryTtl).

  • Caller / auth: anyone.
  • Errors: LeaseNotFound, LeaseAlreadySettled.
  • Notes: the extension can only raise the entry's lifetime, never lower it, and stops once the remaining term is exhausted: a long-expired lease is bumped by about two days at a time, not by its original term. A settled lease is rejected because its funds have already moved.

docs.title: LeaseStatus and the settled flag
docs.text:
LeaseStatus::of (contracts/registry/src/types.rs) reads exactly two fields:

if lease.settled { LeaseStatus::Settled }
else if now >= lease.expires_at { LeaseStatus::Expired }
else { LeaseStatus::Active }

settled is the escrow-release flag, not the reason the funds left. settle_lease sets it after a provider payout, and revoke_expired_lease sets it after a full refund, so both terminal paths report Settled (discriminant 2) and lease_status cannot tell them apart. The same collapse shows up in the error: LeaseAlreadySettled (7) means "already settled or revoked".

docs.title: Telling the two paths apart
docs.text:
used_calls is written by settle_lease only — revoke_expired_lease never touches it — so for most leases one read separates the paths:

Signal after settled == true Meaning used_calls > 0 settle_lease paid the provider for that many calls. used_calls == 0 ambiguous: a revoke, or a settle reported with verified_calls = 0. lease_revoked exists for this lease_id the consumer reclaimed the deposit. lease_settled exists for this lease_id the provider settled; read payout/refund.

The ambiguity is real and not an edge case: a provider that could not serve a lease at all settles it with verified_calls = 0, which refunds the whole deposit and leaves used_calls at 0 — a storage state identical to a revocation. Only the published event distinguishes the two, so anything that reports provider reliability or revenue must consume the event stream rather than poll get_lease: see Topics, payloads and filters.

docs.title: Status by lifecycle event
docs.text:
Worked terms: rate_per_call = 1_000_000, allocated_calls = 500, duration_secs = 3600, so locked_deposit = 500_000_000.

Lifecycle point settled used_calls lease_status remaining_calls locked_balance create_lease false 0 Active 500 500_000_000 120 calls served, not yet expired false 0 Active 500 500_000_000 settle_lease(320) before expiry rejected — LeaseNotSettleable 0 Active 500 500_000_000 expiry reached, nobody acted false 0 Expired 0 500_000_000 settle_lease(320) inside the 24h grace true 320 Settled 0 0 settle_lease(500) (all calls used) true 500 Settled 0 0 settle_lease(0) inside the 24h grace true 0 Settled 0 0 revoke_expired_lease after the grace true 0 Settled 0 0

Two things to read off that table:

  • used_calls and remaining_calls describe the settled allotment, not live usage. Providers report call counts at settlement, so mid-term rows keep used_calls = 0; per-request enforcement is the provider's own counter, bounded on chain by allocated_calls (see the verification pipeline).
  • The last four rows are indistinguishable by lease_status alone. Distinguish them by used_calls, then by the event, never by the status code.

docs.title: Read-only views
docs.text:
These require no authorization, and none of them extends a TTL. An extension bills the caller for rent across the whole extended horizon, so a "view" that performed one could not be used to price a read.

View Signature Returns get_admin (env) -> Result<Address, Error> stored admin, else NotInitialized get_token (env) -> Result<Address, Error> escrow token, else TokenNotSet get_pending_upgrade (env) -> Option<PendingUpgrade> queued hash and execution ledger, if any version (env) -> String version embedded by contractmeta! service_count (env) -> u64 total services ever registered lease_count (env) -> u64 total leases ever created get_service (env, service_id: u64) -> Result<Service, Error> the Service, else ServiceNotFound get_lease (env, lease_id: u64) -> Result<Lease, Error> the Lease, else LeaseNotFound lease_status (env, lease_id: u64) -> Result<LeaseStatus, Error> derived status at current ledger time remaining_calls (env, lease_id: u64) -> Result<u32, Error> calls left; 0 once settled or expired locked_balance (env, lease_id: u64) -> Result<i128, Error> locked_deposit; 0 once settled

remaining_calls returns 0 as soon as the lease expires, even if calls were never consumed. A caller that wants the raw allotment should read get_lease().allocated_calls.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Events are part of the ABI. Each event name is a Symbol topic, followed by the #[topic] fields; the payload is a map keyed by field name.

Every payload carries schema_version (EVENT_SCHEMA_VERSION, currently 1) as its first map key. Topics are frozen: a version is never added as a topic, because topics are positional and indexers filter on them.

Event Topics Payload fields registry_initialized — schema_version, admin escrow_token_set — schema_version, admin, token service_registered service_id schema_version, provider, rate_per_call, endpoint_hash service_status_changed service_id schema_version, provider, is_active lease_created lease_id schema_version, service_id, consumer, allocated_calls, expires_at, locked_deposit lease_settled lease_id schema_version, provider, verified_calls, payout, refund lease_revoked lease_id schema_version, consumer, refund contract_upgraded — schema_version, admin, new_wasm_hash

See integration.md for how to branch on the version.

stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger 123456

docs.title: Storage layout
docs.text:
pub enum DataKey {
    Admin,          // instance
    Token,          // instance
    ServiceCount,   // instance
    LeaseCount,     // instance
    Service(u64),   // persistent
    Lease(u64),     // persistent
    PendingUpgrade, // instance (appended)
}

#[contracttype] enums encode as a SCV_VEC whose first element is an SCV_SYMBOL variant name — so DataKey::Lease(7) is the wire key Vec[Symbol("Lease"), u64(7)]. This matters if you read contract data directly with getContractData; see the developer guide.

docs.title: Storage classes and TTL policies
docs.text:
Soroban expires storage: every key below has a lifetime, and when it runs out the host deletes the entry. Two operations keep an entry alive — a save on a write path (save_service, save_lease, the instance writes) and an explicit bump (bump_service, bump_lease, documented under Storage maintenance). Reads do neither. That split is deliberate and it is priced: an extension bills the caller for rent across the whole extended horizon, so a view that bumped what it read would turn a free lookup into a large fee. test_bump_lease_is_where_the_rent_lives pins the difference — the pure read costs 113 stroops, bump_lease costs 48,798, of which 48,684 is the rent for the horizon it just bought.

The numbers come from contracts/registry/src/storage.rs:

Constant Ledgers Wall clock at 5s blocks LEDGER_CLOSE_SECS — 5 seconds LEDGER_BUMP_THRESHOLD 17_280 1 day — below this remaining life, a save or a bump extends the entry LEDGER_BUMP_EXTEND 518_400 30 days — the horizon instance and Service entries are extended to MAX_ENTRY_TTL_LEDGERS 1_555_200 90 days — the ceiling every extension in this module is clamped to

The last row is a policy bound rather than a network constant. ttl_ceiling returns min(MAX_ENTRY_TTL_LEDGERS, env.storage().max_ttl()), so no call can ask for more than 90 days of lifetime and no call can contradict a network that publishes a smaller maxEntryTtl (6,312,000 ledgers on Pubnet and Testnet). Because create_lease caps a lease at 30 days, the clamp never truncates a well-formed lease; what it bounds is an entry whose expires_at says something else — one migrated in by an upgrade, or created after a future raise of MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS.

Key Class Holds Extended by TTL policy If it is never extended Admin Instance Address of the protocol admin init, set_token (only when the token actually changes; a repeat call is a no-op), register_service, create_lease — each via extend_instance_ttl extend to 30 days, clamped, when less than 1 day is left The whole contract instance entry is evicted: the id stops resolving, and admin, token and both counters are gone with it. Token Instance SEP-41 escrow token Address as Admin as Admin as Admin. Reads answer TokenNotSet, writes answer NotInitialized long before eviction, so a missing value is a bug report, not a normal state. ServiceCount Instance u64, next service id as Admin as Admin as Admin. It resets to 0 on a fresh instance, which is why id monotonicity is only guaranteed within one live instance. LeaseCount Instance u64, next lease id as Admin as Admin as ServiceCount. Service(u64) Persistent Service struct (provider, rate, endpoint hash, active) save_service — so register_service and set_service_active; create_lease via extend_service_ttl; and bump_service. Not get_service, settle_lease (which reads the service), or any view extend to 30 days, clamped, when less than 1 day is left The entry is dropped and every call naming that id answers ServiceNotFound (4) — including settle_lease on leases that are still live. Nothing resurrects it: re-registering mints a new id, so the old leases are orphaned. The defence is bump_service, which needs no authorisation and is paid for by whoever calls it. Lease(u64) Persistent Lease struct (allotted and used calls, expires_at, locked_deposit, settled) save_lease — so create_lease, settle_lease, revoke_expired_lease; and bump_lease. Not the get_lease, lease_status, remaining_calls, locked_balance views lease-specific: see the next section The entry is dropped and get_lease answers LeaseNotFound (6). Settlement and the consumer's refund path both begin by reading the lease, so an evicted lease can be neither settled nor refunded. bump_lease prevents that while the entry still exists and can do nothing after it is gone.

A registry that is deployed and then left unused is not kept alive by reads: settle_lease, revoke_expired_lease, upgrade, bump_service, bump_lease and every view leave the instance horizon alone. Instance eviction is a redeploy event, and Networks treats it as one.

docs.title: The lease-specific extension
docs.text:
save_lease and extend_lease_ttl (the body of bump_lease) do not use the generic 30-day horizon. Both call storage::lease_ttl_extend, which sizes the entry to the time the lease can actually be acted on:

ledgers = (remaining_term_secs + SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS) / LEDGER_CLOSE_SECS
          + LEDGER_BUMP_THRESHOLD
          then clamped to ttl_ceiling

remaining_term_secs is expires_at - now, saturating at zero, so the result covers the lease term, then the 24-hour provider settlement window, then one extra day of buffer for the consumer's revoke_expired_lease call. Worked examples:

Lease Extension Entry lives 1 hour, fresh 35_280 ledgers ~2 days 7 days, fresh 155_520 ledgers ~9 days 30 days (MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS), fresh 552_960 ledgers ~32 days already expired 34_560 ledgers 2 days — the grace window plus the buffer expires_at far past any legitimate term 1_555_200 ledgers 90 days — the clamp, not the term

The fourth row is why bump_lease is safe to expose permissionlessly: once a lease's horizon is in the past the ask stops shrinking. An expired lease is extended about two days at a time, never by its original term, so bumping the tail of a lease is a small explicit payment rather than an accidental re-buy of months of rent.

Three properties make this safe rather than merely cheap:

  • Bounded. create_lease rejects durations above MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS (DurationTooLong, 16) and every ask passes through ttl_ceiling, so a caller cannot inflate the extension and rent stays predictable. bump_lease takes only a lease_id: the horizon comes from the lease's own expires_at, never from the caller.
  • Never shorter than the money is locked. The entry outlives expires_at + SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS, which is the last moment anyone can claim against the lease. A deposit cannot outlive the record that authorises paying it — the invariant docs/security.md states as "every lease has a consumer path to a full refund, for its entire TTL".
  • Only ever forward. Soroban's extend_ttl raises liveUntilLedgerSeq and cannot lower it, so a bump can never shorten a lease somebody already paid for (test_bump_lease_cannot_shorten_a_live_lease).

One asymmetry is worth stating plainly: keeping an entry alive is not the same as being able to read it. bump_lease refuses a settled lease with LeaseAlreadySettled (7) because its funds have already moved and extending it would only grow state, and bump_service answers ServiceNotFound (4) for an unknown id so that nobody pays rent for an entry that was never there.

The old behaviour — extending every lease to the generic 30-day horizon on every read — charged a one-hour lease thirty days of Soroban rent, and made the read path expensive. That is why the calculation is per-lease, and why reads no longer do it.

docs.text:
Codes are part of the ABI. New variants are appended; existing numbers are never reused.

Code Variant Meaning 1 AlreadyInitialized init called twice 2 NotInitialized registry has no admin 3 Unauthorized caller is not the required actor 4 ServiceNotFound no service with that id 5 ServiceInactive service is paused 6 LeaseNotFound no lease with that id 7 LeaseAlreadySettled lease already settled or revoked 8 LeaseNotSettleable not expired and not fully consumed 9 LeaseNotExpired revoke before expiry 10 RevokeWindowNotElapsed revoke inside the 24h grace window 11 InvalidCalls zero calls, or more than allocated 12 InvalidDuration zero duration 13 InvalidRate non-positive rate 14 TokenNotSet escrow token not configured 15 Overflow checked arithmetic failed 16 DurationTooLong lease duration above MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS 17 DepositTooLarge deposit above MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT 18 AttestorNotConfigured settle_lease_attested on a service with no attestor 19 AttestationRequired plain settle_lease on a service that requires one 20 AttestationMismatch attestation does not match the lease, service or calls 21 AttestationStale attestation's valid_until has passed 22 NoPendingUpgrade cancel_upgrade/execute_upgrade with no proposal 23 UpgradeDelayNotElapsed execute_upgrade before execute_after

  -- register_service \

# create a lease

docs.title: MockToken (test only)
docs.text:
contracts/mock_token implements a minimal SEP-41 surface — init, mint, transfer, transfer_from, approve, allowance, balance, decimals (7), name, symbol, admin — with an unlimited mint.

It exists so local sandboxes do not depend on a live SAC, but it must never be deployed to a network holding value. The registry's own tests escrow against the real Stellar Asset Contract (register_stellar_asset_contract_v2).

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
Deploying KeyLease is a short, strictly ordered sequence of stellar contract commands against a Stellar network. Steps 2–5 each depend on the previous one, so the whole thing is scripted:

SOURCE_ACCOUNT=keylease-admin ./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh

To create and fund the identity as well (Testnet only):

KEYLEASE_GENERATE_KEY=1 SOURCE_ACCOUNT=keylease-admin ./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh

The script never deploys mock_token. That token has an unlimited mint and is for tests and local sandboxes only.

docs.title: What the script does
docs.text:
1. cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all
2. stellar contract deploy   <registry wasm>  -> REGISTRY contract id
3. stellar contract invoke -- init            --admin  <ADMIN>
4. stellar contract invoke -- set_token       --admin <ADMIN> --token <TOKEN>
5. stellar contract invoke -- register_service --provider <P> \
                              --rate_per_call <R> --endpoint_hash <H>

Then it re-reads get_service to confirm the write landed, and prints a block you can paste into .env:

KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID=C...
KEYLEASE_SERVICE_ID=1
KEYLEASE_TOKEN_ADDRESS=...
KEYLEASE_NETWORK=testnet
KEYLEASE_RPC_URL=https://soroban-testnet.stellar.org

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Variable Default Meaning SOURCE_ACCOUNT keylease-admin stellar CLI identity used to sign NETWORK testnet network name from your CLI config REGISTRY_ALIAS keylease-registry contract alias saved locally ADMIN address of SOURCE_ACCOUNT registry admin PROVIDER ADMIN owner of the demo service TOKEN native SAC on NETWORK escrow token RATE_PER_CALL 1000000 0.1 XLM at 7 decimals ENDPOINT_HASH sha256("<PROVIDER>:keylease-demo") 32-byte commitment KEYLEASE_GENERATE_KEY unset 1 to generate + Friendbot-fund the identity

docs.title: Doing it manually
docs.text:
The script is the supported path, but the raw commands are:

# 0. identity
stellar keys generate keylease-admin --network testnet --fund

# 1. build
rustup target add wasm32v1-none
cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --package keylease-registry

# 2. deploy
REGISTRY=$(stellar contract deploy \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet \
  --alias keylease-registry)

# 3. initialize
ADMIN=$(stellar keys address keylease-admin)
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- init --admin "$ADMIN"

# 4. configure the escrow token (native SAC here)
TOKEN=$(stellar contract id asset --network testnet --asset native)
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- set_token --admin "$ADMIN" --token "$TOKEN"

# 5. publish a service
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- register_service \
    --provider "$ADMIN" \
    --rate_per_call 1000000 \
    --endpoint_hash 0707070707070707070707070707070707070707070707070707070707070707

--send=yes is required for the state-changing invocations. Without it the CLI only simulates. The -- before the function name is required.

docs.title: Verifying a deployment
docs.text:
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- version
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- get_admin
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- get_token
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- get_service --service_id 1
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- service_count

version is embedded by contractmeta!, so it proves which release is live. The contract id itself is in the registry: see Deployments, and the explorer link for that network in Networks.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
The contract is upgradeable in place through the Soroban deployer; the contract id, storage and balances are preserved. Because the old storage carries over, the steps must run in order and the result must be checked, so they are scripted:

./scripts/upgrade.sh --contract-id C... --admin keylease-admin

Both flags are required and have no defaults: the script will not guess which contract to replace or which key signs for it. --admin is a stellar CLI identity; its address is passed to upgrade --admin and must equal the live get_admin, which the script checks before it sends anything.

docs.title: What the upgrade script does
docs.text:
0. get_admin, version                     -> confirm the signer is the admin, record the live version
1. cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --package keylease-registry
2. stellar contract upload  <registry wasm> -> Wasm hash (must equal sha256 of the built file)
3. stellar contract invoke -- upgrade      --admin <ADMIN> --new_wasm_hash <HASH>
4. stellar contract invoke -- version      -> must equal [workspace.package] version in Cargo.toml

It then prints the Wasm hash, the version before and after, and the stellar events command (with the contract_upgraded topic filter and the ledger it started from) to confirm the upgrade event. It exits non-zero when:

  • --contract-id or --admin is missing, or the id is not a C... contract id;
  • the identity is not the registry admin;
  • the live contract already reports the workspace version — bump [workspace.package] version first, or pass --allow-same-version to re-install the same release deliberately;
  • the uploaded hash differs from the local build;
  • version() after the upgrade does not equal the workspace version.
Flag Default Meaning --contract-id required (env CONTRACT_ID) registry contract to upgrade --admin required (env ADMIN_IDENTITY) stellar CLI identity of the registry admin --network testnet (env NETWORK) network name from your CLI config --allow-same-version off proceed when the live version already equals the workspace version --yes off skip the confirmation prompt (required on a non-interactive shell)

REGISTRY=C... SOURCE_ACCOUNT=keylease-admin ./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh --upgrade still works and hands off to scripts/upgrade.sh.

docs.title: Upgrading manually
docs.text:
The raw commands the script wraps are:

# 1. upload the new Wasm and print its hash
WASM_HASH=$(stellar contract upload \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet)

# 2. propose the upgrade (admin auth); read back the hash and execution ledger
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- propose_upgrade \
    --admin $ADMIN --new_wasm_hash "$WASM_HASH"
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --network testnet -- get_pending_upgrade

# 3. wait until ledger.timestamp() >= execute_after (24h), then install
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- execute_upgrade --admin $ADMIN

# 4. confirm the new version and watch the event
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- version
stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger>

Guard rails for an upgrade: keep the storage layout unchanged, append error codes instead of renumbering, and keep event names and payload fields backwards-compatible. The execute_after timestamp and proposed hash are public via get_pending_upgrade and upgrade_proposed; announce them so clients can exit in time. Settle or revoke in-flight leases before changing token semantics. See Security and the design note.

docs.title: Upgrading safety checklist
docs.text:
An upgrade replaces the code but keeps the contract id, so every stored entry written by the old Wasm is still there when the new Wasm runs. The new code does not get a clean slate — it gets your users' escrow. Work the checklist in order.

1. Invariants the new Wasm must preserve. These are the reasons the guard rails above exist; the full layout is in Storage layout.

Invariant Why an upgrade can silently break it DataKey variant names and arities: Admin, Token, ServiceCount, LeaseCount, Service(u64), Lease(u64) A #[contracttype] enum key encodes as Vec[Symbol("<variant>"), …], so renaming Lease to Leases orphans every existing entry. The registry then reads LeaseNotFound on leases that still hold escrow. Stored value shapes for Service and Lease Entries decode by field name and type. Renaming used_calls, retyping locked_deposit, or removing settled reinterprets or loses live records. Field presence, not field order, for structs Old entries are read by key, so adding a field is safe only if the accessor tolerates its absence in entries written before the upgrade. Error codes, append-only (1–16 today) Callers and indexers branch on the number; a reused code changes what a past transaction meant. Event names, topics and payload fields, append-only They are the indexing ABI. Dropping a #[topic] field shifts every subscriber's filter, including the base64 segments in Topics, payloads and filters. LeaseStatus discriminants (0/1/2) Returned by lease_status and cached by clients. The settled-before-token-call ordering in settle_lease and revoke_expired_lease It is the double-payout guard; reordering it behind a transfer reintroduces the re-entrancy bug the suite proves closed. The lease TTL policy covers term + 24 h grace + read buffer If a shorter policy evicts a lease entry while escrow is still locked, the consumer's revoke path disappears. MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS never lowered below an in-flight lease's term Existing leases stay settleable; lowering the cap for new leases is additive, lowering it retroactively is not.

2. Record the live state before you touch anything.

# version, counters and the exact Wasm you are replacing
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- version
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- service_count
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- lease_count
sha256sum target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm

Keep the highest pre-upgrade lease_id and note the current ledger: it is the --start-ledger for the replay in step 5.

3. Upgrade. Upload, install, and keep the hash the deployer returned. ./scripts/upgrade.sh --contract-id $REGISTRY --admin keylease-admin runs this step and step 4 together; the raw commands are:

WASM_HASH=$(stellar contract upload \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet)
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- upgrade --admin $ADMIN --new_wasm_hash "$WASM_HASH"

4. Compare version(). The embedded metadata must move; a build that did not bump the workspace version installed new code that still reports the old one.

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- version
stellar contract info meta --id $REGISTRY --network testnet

version must equal the release you intended, and name must still be KeyLeaseRegistry. Then re-read one lease and one service created before the upgrade and diff the field values against step 2 — identical expires_at, allocated_calls, locked_deposit and settled is what proves the stored shapes were not reinterpreted.

5. Replay the events across the boundary.

stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger-from-step-2>

Expect exactly one contract_upgraded carrying the new_wasm_hash from step 3, with nothing else in that transaction; the counters must be unchanged across it (service_count and lease_count before equals after — an upgrade mints no leases); and every lease_created before the upgrade must still have a terminal lease_settled or lease_revoked after it. If a pre-upgrade lease that was Active now reverts on settle_lease, stop: the new Wasm is not storage-safe.

6. Only then resume traffic, and record the outcome — the new version, Wasm hash and upgrade ledger — in Deployments, which ties a listed address to a revision.

Rollback. upgrade is symmetric: install the previous Wasm's hash the same way. It is only safe while the new build has written nothing the old one cannot read, so a new DataKey variant or new field is a one-way door the moment it is used.

docs.title: Multisig admin deployment and upgrades
docs.text: In production, operators should configure a cold or multi-signature account as the registry admin to prevent a single compromised key from executing unauthorized contract upgrades or token modifications.

docs.title: 1. Initialization with a multisig admin
docs.text:
Any funded account can build and deploy the contract Wasm. When initializing the registry, pass the multi-signature account address (G_MULTISIG...) as the --admin parameter:

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account deployer \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- init --admin "$MULTISIG_ADMIN"

Once initialized, all functions requiring admin privileges (set_token and upgrade) call admin.require_auth(), delegating authorization enforcement to the Stellar host.

docs.title: 2. Multi-party upgrade workflow
docs.text:
Upgrades with a multisig admin are coordinated through transaction envelopes:

  1. Upload the new Wasm: Any account can upload the compiled bytecode to obtain its hash: 

    WASM_HASH=$(stellar contract upload \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account deployer --network testnet)

  2. Construct the unsigned invocation transaction: 

    stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" \
  --source-account "$MULTISIG_ADMIN" \
  --network testnet \
  --build-only \
  -- upgrade --admin "$MULTISIG_ADMIN" --new_wasm_hash "$WASM_HASH" > upgrade_tx.xdr

  3. Collect signatures from signers: Each required co-signer signs the envelope until the cumulative signature weight meets or exceeds the admin account's threshold: 

    stellar tx sign --network testnet --source-account signer-alice upgrade_tx.xdr > signed_1.xdr
stellar tx sign --network testnet --source-account signer-bob signed_1.xdr > signed_threshold.xdr

  4. Submit the fully-signed transaction: 

    stellar tx send --network testnet signed_threshold.xdr

docs.title: Host-level auth guarantees
docs.text:
• What the contract enforces: The contract checks admin.require_auth(). If the accumulated signature weight does not meet the Stellar account's configured threshold, the host rejects the transaction before contract invocation occurs.
  • What the contract cannot enforce: The contract does not inspect individual signer identities, weights, or whether the signer set is 2-of-3 versus 1-of-1. Those rules live entirely within the Stellar account configuration.

docs.title: Post-deploy
docs.text:

docs.title: Deployment economics (Testnet)
docs.text: The Wasm upload reserves on-chain code rent (~3,557 XLM for this build at the current Testnet settings). Lease creation pays storage rent as part of the transaction resource fee: the host enforces a minimum persistent TTL (~7 days on Testnet), so the first lease (which also funded the contract's own SAC balance entry) cost ~20 XLM, a following 10-call lease cost ~5.6 XLM, and settlement is a few thousand stroops. Mainnet rent parameters differ; size allotments against real fees before quoting per-call prices.

docs.title: Verifying a listed address
docs.text:
The registry can be checked without trusting this page: the Wasm carries contractmeta!, and the configured token and admin are public views.

stellar contract invoke --id <ID> --source-account <funded-account> --network testnet -- version
stellar contract invoke --id <ID> --source-account <funded-account> --network testnet -- get_admin
stellar contract invoke --id <ID> --source-account <funded-account> --network testnet -- get_token

# lifecycle history, straight from the ledger
stellar events --id <ID> --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger>

version() must match the release this page claims, get_admin() must be the documented admin, and escrow_token_set / service_registered events must appear at the recorded deployment ledger.

The deployed Wasm is reproducible from this tree — its hash matches stellar contract info hash:

cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all
sha256sum target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm
# 5362d4cb866a0405f17d1adfe8179e63afaca8a7dc741df3c3b87ee0ab75146a

docs.title: Recording a deployment
docs.text:
1. Run ./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh.
  2. Copy the printed values into the Testnet table above, including the contract version.
  3. Record the deployment ledger so stellar events can be replayed.
  4. Commit the change and tag the release so the addresses are tied to a specific revision.

docs.title: Recording a post-reset deployment
docs.text:
A Testnet reset (2–4 times a year, 17:00 UTC) wipes the ledger, so this table is stale from the moment it happens and a reader can be pointed at a contract id that no longer exists. The operator sequence is in Networks — After a Testnet reset; what changes here is only the record:

Field After a reset KeyLeaseRegistry new id — from the script output, never from memory. Contract version, Wasm hash Whatever this build produced. Unchanged only if you deployed the same commit. Contract created, init, set_token, register_service All new ledgers and tx links. The pre-reset history is gone, so replay starts at the new Contract created ledger. Escrow token (native SAC) unchanged — derived from the passphrase, which a reset does not alter. Re-derive it to prove it: stellar contract id asset --network testnet --asset native. Admin / provider / demo consumer unchanged addresses, but the accounts themselves were wiped and must be re-funded before they can sign. Demo service_id Back to 1. ServiceCount is instance storage and the instance is new, so ids restart rather than continue. Any consumer still holding an old id is calling a service that does not exist.

Two things to do before merging the update:

  1. Prove the old id is dead. stellar contract info fetch --id <OLD> --network testnet and … -- version must both fail; the event stream must answer empty. If version() replies, you are on the wrong RPC or the reset has not landed yet.
  2. Keep the superseded id in history, not in the table. The old id belongs in the commit that replaces it (git log -p docs/deployments.md), not in a "previous deployments" section — a second live-looking address on this page is exactly the fake-contract-id risk Security warns about.

docs.title: Developer guide
docs.text: How to build, test, upgrade and extend the KeyLease Soroban contracts.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Tool Version Notes Rust 1.84+ rustup install stable Wasm target wasm32v1-none rustup target add wasm32v1-none components rustfmt, clippy rustup component add rustfmt clippy Stellar CLI latest only needed to deploy, invoke, read events or upgrade on a network Node.js >= 20.11 only if you build your own JS client against Soroban RPC

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/KeyLease-Security/keylease-core
cd keylease-core
rustup target add wasm32v1-none

cargo build --all
cargo test --all

docs.title: The commands CI runs
docs.text:
These five are the definition of "green". Run all five before opening a PR.

cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo clippy --target wasm32v1-none --release --all -- -D warnings
cargo test --all
cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all

CI also runs a cargo-deny dependency policy check (deny.toml) and a ClamAV malware scan over the checkout and the built Wasm artifacts. CI job names are Format, Clippy, Test, Build (wasm32v1-none), Dependency Policy and Malware Scan — these are the required status checks in branch protection.

docs.title: Project layout
docs.text: Path Purpose contracts/registry/src/lib.rs Entry points, contractmeta!, upgrade, protocol lifecycle. contracts/registry/src/events.rs Typed #[contractevent] payloads. contracts/registry/src/types.rs Service, Lease, LeaseStatus. contracts/registry/src/storage.rs DataKey layout, TTL policy, accessors. contracts/registry/src/errors.rs Stable Error codes (never reuse a number). contracts/registry/src/test.rs Lifecycle, SAC, events, upgrade and re-entrancy tests. contracts/mock_token/ Test/sandbox SEP-41 token. scripts/deploy-testnet.sh Sequential testnet deploy and upgrade. scripts/check-no-std.sh Checks the release Wasm is built without std and crates forbid unsafe. scripts/create-issues.sh Batch Wave backlog creation. scripts/setup-repo.sh Topics, labels, branch protection.
