Variable Used by Meaning KEYLEASE_NETWORK scripts, clients testnet / mainnet / futurenet / local KEYLEASE_RPC_URL scripts, clients Soroban RPC endpoint KEYLEASE_NETWORK_PASSPHRASE clients passphrase used to sign transactions KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID scripts, clients deployed KeyLeaseRegistry id KEYLEASE_SERVICE_ID clients service a consumer acquires from KEYLEASE_TOKEN_ADDRESS tooling SEP-41 / SAC escrow token KEYLEASE_ADMIN / KEYLEASE_PROVIDER / KEYLEASE_CONSUMER tooling Stellar addresses KEYLEASE_RATE_PER_CALL register_service stroops per call KEYLEASE_ENDPOINT_HASH register_service 64 hex chars (32 bytes)

Never commit secret seeds. .env is gitignored.

docs.title: Adding a new entry point
docs.text:
1. Add the variant(s) to errors.rs (append, never renumber).
  2. Add any new DataKey variants to storage.rs with a documented TTL policy.
  3. Implement the entry point in lib.rs, documenting auth + preconditions.
  4. Add a typed event in events.rs and publish it after the state is persisted.
  5. Add tests covering the happy path and each failure/refund path, plus the emitted event.
  6. Update the interface and event tables in README.md and docs/contract-reference.md.

docs.title: Code standards
docs.text:
• #![no_std] — no std in contract code; the target is wasm32v1-none.
  • All token math is checked; map failures to Error::Overflow.
  • Authenticate actors with require_auth() on the address you represent.
  • Follow checks-effects-interactions. Persist settled (or the equivalent) before any cross-contract call.
  • Guard money paths with the settled check first.
  • Bound storage. Every persistent key needs a TTL policy and, if user input controls its lifetime, an upper bound.
  • No unbounded loops over user-supplied collections.
  • Errors over panics.
  • Never reuse an error code.
  • Emit events for every state transition; never put secrets in one.

docs.title: Testing conventions
docs.text:
Use env.mock_all_auths() for happy paths and try_* client methods to assert specific errors:

assert_eq!(
    client.try_settle_lease(&provider, &lease_id, &11),
    Err(Ok(Error::InvalidCalls))
);

Event tests compare the emitted topics and payload with the event type generated by #[contractevent]:

assert_single_event(
    &env,
    &registry_id,
    &LeaseSettled { lease_id, provider, verified_calls, payout, refund },
);

The suite also deploys the real Stellar Asset Contract as the escrow token (env.register_stellar_asset_contract_v2), and installs a hostile SEP-41 token that re-enters settle_lease to prove the double-settlement guard holds. Keep both patterns when adding money paths.

Every security-sensitive change needs an adversarial test — an attempt to steal, strand, or double-spend.

docs.title: Releasing a version
docs.text: A release is four things: a version bump, a notes page, a check run and an annotated tag. Nothing in .github/workflows/ publishes a crate, builds a GitHub Release or cuts a tag — ci.yml only gates commits and docs.yml only builds the site on push to main — so the steps below are the whole process.

docs.title: 1. Bump the version
docs.text:
Cargo.toml carries the only version this repository reports. Both crates inherit it (version.workspace = true), so one edit covers the workspace — but two more files have to follow it.

File What changes Cargo.toml [workspace.package] version = "X.Y.Z" contracts/registry/Cargo.toml the version = "X.Y.Z" pin on the keylease-mock-token dev-dependency Cargo.lock the keylease-registry and keylease-mock-token entries — regenerate with cargo check --all and commit the diff

No other file carries a version string, because the version reaches the rest of the system through the build:

  • contractmeta!(key = "version", val = env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION")) embeds the new value in the Wasm, so stellar contract info meta reports it.
  • version() reads that same value, so the on-chain contract identifies itself after the upgrade — the check in Deployment.

Use the convention the existing releases already follow. 0.x.0 is a release that changes what the world sees — a new entry point, a new event, a new error code, new storage. 0.x.1 is a release that changes none of those (v0.2.1 only changed the lease TTL policy). Error codes are append-only, so a new code alone is never a major-version event.

docs.title: 2. Write the notes page
docs.text:
Add docs/releases/vX.Y.Z.md, then register it in both tables of contents — mkdocs.yml under nav: → Project: and docs/SUMMARY.md under ## Project. The newest page keeps the Release notes label and the previous ones are relabelled to their version:

  - Project:
      - Deployments: deployments.md
      - Release notes: releases/v0.2.2.md   # new
      - v0.2.1: releases/v0.2.1.md          # relabelled
      - v0.2.0: releases/v0.2.0.md
      - v0.1.0: releases/v0.1.0.md

Copy the shape from an existing page rather than inventing one:

Example What it shows v0.2.1 a behavior-only patch: the problem it solved, a short "What changed", compatibility stated as "no ABI, event, storage-key or error-code changes" v0.2.0 an additive release: new events and upgrade, a full "Interface at this tag" table, and an "Upgrading from v0.1.0" section v0.1.0 the first release, and the banner pattern a superseded page uses to point at the current interface

A notes page needs these sections, in this order:

  1. Heading and lead — # keylease-core vX.Y.Z then one paragraph saying what the release is and, when there is a reason, why it exists.
  2. Highlights or What changed — one bullet per user-visible change, each naming the entry point, constant or error code it touched.
  3. Contracts — the package → Wasm table.
  4. Interface at this tag — the entry points and their auth requirements, so the page stays readable after the reference moves on.
  5. Compatibility — Rust, soroban-sdk, Wasm target, the error-code range, and an explicit statement about storage keys and events.
  6. Upgrading from vX.Y.Z — required whenever a deployed network is running an older build; say whether upgrade is safe in place.
  7. Known limitations, Verification (the four commands), License.

Never put a secret, seed or raw credential in a notes page — including a deployer's secret key. Addresses and ledger numbers are fine and useful.

docs.title: 3. Run the checks a release is gated on
docs.text:
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo clippy --target wasm32v1-none --release --all -- -D warnings
cargo test --all
cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all
./scripts/check-no-std.sh --no-build
cargo deny check
./scripts/scan-malware.sh
pip install -r requirements-docs.txt && mkdocs build --strict

The first four are the CI jobs every commit must pass, and check-no-std.sh runs inside the Build (wasm32v1-none) job; cargo deny check and ./scripts/scan-malware.sh are the Dependency Policy and Malware Scan jobs run locally. mkdocs build --strict is the one that bites at release time: the docs workflow only runs on main, so a notes page missing from nav: or a dangling anchor goes red after the release commit has landed.

docs.title: 4. Tag the release commit on main
docs.text:
Tag the merge-base commit on main that carries both the version bump and the notes page — not a branch tip that has not merged. v0.1.0 is an annotated tag, so stay annotated:

git fetch origin
git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "keylease-core vX.Y.Z" origin/main
git push origin vX.Y.Z

The tag is what makes the recorded hashes meaningful: it is the revision anyone can rebuild from to reproduce the deployed Wasm.

docs.title: 5. Record the artifacts
docs.text:
Deploying is covered in Deployment; what a release must record is in Deployments, whose Recording a deployment steps this table feeds.

Artifact How to obtain it Where it is recorded Contract id stellar contract deploy prints it Testnet table, KeyLeaseRegistry Built Wasm digest sha256sum target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm "Verifying a listed address" On-chain Wasm hash stellar contract upload prints it; stellar contract info hash --id $REGISTRY reads it back Testnet table, "Wasm hash" Version, as the chain sees it … -- version and stellar contract info meta --id $REGISTRY Testnet table + "On-chain metadata" (rssdkver included) Deploy-ledger trail ledger and tx hash for init, set_token, register_service, or the upgrade Testnet table rows Pre/post counters service_count, lease_count, get_service, get_lease release notes "Verified on-chain" bullet Signer addresses admin, provider, demo consumer, escrow token Testnet table Source revision the tag cut in step 4 Testnet table, "Deployed from"

The built digest and the on-chain hash are the same value only if the build is reproducible: check out the tag, run cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all and compare against stellar contract info hash. If they differ, the release is not verifiable from source — say so in the notes page rather than recording a hash you cannot reproduce.

docs.title: Upgrading a deployment
docs.text:
stellar contract upload \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account admin --network testnet

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account admin --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- propose_upgrade --admin $ADMIN --new_wasm_hash <hash-from-upload>

# inspect the recorded hash and execution ledger timestamp
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --network testnet -- get_pending_upgrade

# after the 24h delay has elapsed (the contract rejects earlier calls)
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account admin --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- execute_upgrade --admin $ADMIN

# or abandon the proposal: -- cancel_upgrade --admin $ADMIN

Rules for upgrades:

  • Never change the DataKey layout or the meaning of stored values.
  • Never renumber or reuse an error code.
  • Keep event names and payload fields compatible; add new events for new transitions.
  • Bump the workspace version so version() and contractmeta! change.
  • Settle or revoke in-flight leases before changing token semantics.

docs.title: Reading contract state and events
docs.text:
Clients should prefer the read views and the event stream over raw storage:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet -- get_lease --lease_id 1
stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger 123456

If you must read storage directly, #[contracttype] enums encode as an SCV_VEC whose first element is an SCV_SYMBOL with the variant name:

Logical key Wire key DataKey::Admin Symbol("Admin") DataKey::Lease(7) Vec[Symbol("Lease"), u64(7)] DataKey::Service(3) Vec[Symbol("Service"), u64(3)]

With @stellar/stellar-sdk:

import { xdr, nativeToScVal } from '@stellar/stellar-sdk';

// DataKey::Lease(leaseId)
xdr.ScVal.scvVec([
  xdr.ScVal.scvSymbol('Lease'),
  nativeToScVal(leaseId, { type: 'u64' }),
]);

getContractData returns a scvMap of the Lease struct fields. Decode it as { lease_id, service_id, consumer, allocated_calls, used_calls, expires_at, locked_deposit, settled }. Full details are in the contract reference, and the supported way to verify leases is described in Integration.

docs.title: Deploying
docs.text: See Deployment. scripts/deploy-testnet.sh runs the exact sequence and prints the values a client or indexer needs.

docs.title: Local sandbox walkthrough
docs.text:
The unit suite proves the contract logic inside a simulated ledger. This runs the same lifecycle against a real local network using the Wasm you just built, so you can watch one lease move value end to end.

There is no scripts/deploy-local.sh — the sequence is below, and scripts/deploy-testnet.sh is the Testnet reference for the identical steps. Everything here is stellar 28.1.0 syntax; if your CLI is a different version, re-read the flag with stellar <command> --help rather than assuming.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Requirement Check A running container engine (Docker, Podman or Colima). docker info answers without error. The registry Wasm built. cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all Port 8000 free on localhost. stellar container start local maps 8000:8000 by default; pass -p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT to move it.

docs.title: 1. Start a local network
docs.text:
stellar container start local

This runs the stellar/quickstart image with the node, Soroban RPC, Horizon and a friendbot in one container. The command has no detached mode — note that -d is --docker-host, not Docker's detach flag — so run it in its own terminal and leave it up for the rest of the walkthrough.

local is a built-in CLI network — stellar network ls already lists it, so you do not need stellar network add. It resolves to:

Network passphrase Standalone Network ; February 2017 Soroban RPC http://localhost:8000/rpc Horizon http://localhost:8000 Friendbot http://localhost:8000/friendbot?addr=<ACCOUNT>

You can confirm the RPC is up before going further:

stellar network health --network local
stellar ledger latest --network local

docs.title: 2. Create and fund three identities
docs.text:
Three separate accounts, not one: settle_lease checks service.provider == provider and revoke_expired_lease checks the lease owner. A single account for every role hides exactly the authorisation bugs a sandbox is for.

for who in kl-admin kl-provider kl-consumer; do
  stellar keys generate "$who" --network local --fund
done

--fund works on local too — the CLI posts to the container's own friendbot, the same code path as Testnet. Read a balance back to be sure the account exists:

stellar token balance --id native --account "$(stellar keys address kl-consumer)" --network local

docs.title: 3. Deploy the registry
docs.text:
cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all

REGISTRY=$(stellar contract deploy \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account kl-admin --network local | tail -n1)

docs.title: 4. Initialise, set the escrow token, publish a service
docs.text:
Each step reads what the previous one wrote, which is why the order is fixed.

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-admin \
  --network local --send=yes -- init --admin "$(stellar keys address kl-admin)"

TOKEN=$(stellar contract id asset --network local --asset native)
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-admin \
  --network local --send=yes -- set_token \
     --admin "$(stellar keys address kl-admin)" --token "$TOKEN"

ENDPOINT_HASH=$(printf '%s' "$(stellar keys address kl-provider):local-demo" \
  | shasum -a 256 | awk '{print $1}')

SERVICE_ID=$(stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-provider \
  --network local --send=yes -- register_service \
     --provider "$(stellar keys address kl-provider)" \
     --rate_per_call 1000000 --endpoint_hash "$ENDPOINT_HASH" | tail -n1)

rate_per_call is in stroops, so 1000000 is 0.1 XLM per call.

The native SAC address is derived from the network passphrase, not assigned. On the standalone passphrase it is CDMLFMKMMD7MWZP3FKUBZPVHTUEDLSX4BYGYKH4GCESXYHS3IHQ4EIG4 — re-derive it with the command above rather than copying that value, because your own stellar network add passphrase would give a different address.

docs.title: 5. Create one lease
docs.text:
100 calls at 0.1 XLM escrows 10 XLM:

LEASE_ID=$(stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-consumer \
  --network local --send=yes -- create_lease \
     --consumer "$(stellar keys address kl-consumer)" \
     --service_id "$SERVICE_ID" \
     --requested_calls 100 \
     --duration_secs 120 | tail -n1)

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-consumer \
  --network local -- get_lease --lease_id "$LEASE_ID"
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-consumer \
  --network local -- remaining_calls --lease_id "$LEASE_ID"

Do not approve an allowance first — there is none to grant. create_lease calls transfer(consumer, contract, amount) itself under the consumer's own auth, so the consumer needs a balance, not a permission.

duration_secs is a wall-clock number, and the ledger still advances in real time. 120 seconds is enough to settle an expired lease without leaving the terminal; a day-long lease is not a sandbox demo.

docs.title: 6. Settle it
docs.text:
settle_lease runs when the lease has expired, or when the provider reports full consumption — whichever comes first. Reporting everything immediately is the fastest path through the happy case:

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-provider \
  --network local --send=yes -- settle_lease \
     --provider "$(stellar keys address kl-provider)" \
     --lease_id "$LEASE_ID" --verified_calls 100

Payout and refund must sum to the deposit, so 100 verified of 100 allocated pays the provider 10 XLM and refunds 0. Create a second lease and settle it partially before it expires to see the guard refuse:

OTHER=$(stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-consumer \
  --network local --send=yes -- create_lease \
     --consumer "$(stellar keys address kl-consumer)" \
     --service_id "$SERVICE_ID" --requested_calls 100 --duration_secs 120 | tail -n1)

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-provider \
  --network local --send=yes -- settle_lease \
     --provider "$(stellar keys address kl-provider)" \
     --lease_id "$OTHER" --verified_calls 30
# Error(LeaseNotSettleable) — the lease is live and under-consumed

Wait past duration_secs and the same call succeeds, paying 3 XLM and refunding 7 XLM to the consumer. Verify it with the read views and the token itself:

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-admin --network local \
  -- locked_balance --lease_id "$OTHER"      # 0 once settled
stellar token balance --id native --account "$(stellar keys address kl-provider)" \
  --network local

docs.title: 7. Read the events
docs.text:
Note the ledger sequence before you deploy, then read the whole lifecycle out of the chain afterwards:

stellar ledger latest --network local          # write down the sequence
# ... run steps 3 to 6 ...
stellar events --id "$REGISTRY" --network local --start-ledger <that sequence> -c 50

Expect RegistryInitialized, EscrowTokenSet, ServiceRegistered, LeaseCreated, LeaseSettled. Use -c generously: the default is 10 events, and a full lifecycle plus the token transfers is more than that. Event payloads and their fields are in the contract reference.

docs.title: 8. Keep an entry alive
docs.text:
A local network is the only place this costs nothing to try. Reads never extend a storage entry, so an entry that is looked at but not written ages toward eviction until somebody bumps it explicitly.

# Both are permissionless — any account can pay for any entry's rent.
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-provider --network local \
  -- bump_service --service_id "$SERVICE_ID"

A successful bump is silent: no event, no field changes, and the only effect is a later liveUntilLedgerSeq plus the rent charged into the caller's fee. Lease entries need a lease that can still be acted on, because bump_lease refuses a settled one — so create a third lease and leave it unsettled:

LIVE=$(stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-consumer \
  --network local --send=yes -- create_lease \
     --consumer "$(stellar keys address kl-consumer)" \
     --service_id "$SERVICE_ID" --requested_calls 10 --duration_secs 3600 | tail -n1)

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-consumer --network local \
  -- bump_lease --lease_id "$LIVE"

Then try the two refusals, because they are the reason these calls are safe to leave open to anyone. $LEASE_ID was settled in step 6, so its funds have already moved and extending it would only grow state:

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-provider --network local \
  -- bump_lease --lease_id "$LEASE_ID"         # Error(LeaseAlreadySettled)

# A miss is an error, so nobody pays rent for an entry that is not there.
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-provider --network local \
  -- bump_service --service_id 404             # Error(ServiceNotFound)

bump_lease takes only a lease_id: the horizon comes from the lease's own expires_at and the contract's ceiling, never from the caller. The policy, the per-lease arithmetic and what eviction costs a consumer are in Storage classes and TTL policies.

docs.title: What differs from Testnet
docs.text:
Only the network is different; the contract, its ABI and the step order are not.

Testnet Local sandbox Network flag --network testnet --network local Who operates the network SDF you, in a container you start RPC https://soroban-testnet.stellar.org http://localhost:8000/rpc Friendbot https://friendbot.stellar.org?addr=… http://localhost:8000/friendbot?addr=… Funding an identity stellar keys generate x --network testnet --fund stellar keys generate x --network local --fund — same flag Native SAC address derived from Test SDF Network ; September 2015 derived from Standalone Network ; February 2017; different address Deploy script ./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh no script; the sequence above Contract id lifetime until the next Testnet reset until you stop the container Wiping the ledger 2–4× a year, on SDF's schedule whenever you like: stellar container stop local Value at risk fake XLM none

The commands that are identical are worth stating, because contributors expect to rewrite them: stellar contract deploy, upload, invoke, contract id asset and the --send=yes form all take the same arguments with a different --network. Nothing in contracts/ is network-aware.

docs.title: Teardown
docs.text:
stellar container stop local

# optional: the identities are only seeds on your machine
for who in kl-admin kl-provider kl-consumer; do
  stellar keys rm --force "$who"
done

stellar keys rm takes one name at a time and asks for confirmation unless you pass --force.

stellar container start uses --rm, so stopping the container discards the ledger. Starting it again gives you an empty network with the same passphrase — which means the redeploy you must now do is the same one described in After a Testnet reset, including register_service returning 1 again because ServiceCount lives in instance storage.

docs.title: Using contracts/mock_token instead of the native SAC
docs.text:
The mock token exists so a sandbox does not depend on lumens at all. It has an unlimited mint and must never be configured on a network that holds value — see contract reference.

MOCK=$(stellar contract deploy \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_mock_token.wasm \
  --source-account kl-admin --network local | tail -n1)

stellar contract invoke --id "$MOCK" --source-account kl-admin --network local \
  --send=yes -- init --admin "$(stellar keys address kl-admin)"

# Mint 1000 tokens (7 decimals) to the consumer, then point the registry at it.
stellar contract invoke --id "$MOCK" --source-account kl-admin --network local \
  --send=yes -- mint --to "$(stellar keys address kl-consumer)" --amount 10000000000

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account kl-admin --network local \
  --send=yes -- set_token --admin "$(stellar keys address kl-admin)" --token "$MOCK"

From here the lease steps are unchanged: every money path goes through the token address that set_token stored, so swapping the asset changes nothing else. That indirection is also how you exercise a misbehaving token by hand — point the registry at a contract that reverts or re-enters on transfer. The automated version of exactly that attack is test_reentrant_token_cannot_settle_a_lease_twice in contracts/registry/src/test.rs.

docs.title: Protocol FAQ
docs.text: Frequently asked questions regarding KeyLease escrow mechanics, lifecycles, key management, and network operations.

docs.title: How and when do consumers receive refunds?
docs.text:
Refunds occur under two distinct operational circumstances:

  1. Partial or Zero Usage upon Settlement: When a provider settles a lease via settle_lease, it reports verified_calls. The provider receives verified_calls × rate_per_call, and any unspent remainder of locked_deposit is automatically refunded to the consumer's token balance in the same transaction. If verified_calls == 0, the consumer is refunded 100% of their deposit. See Protocol: Lifecycle and Contract reference: settle_lease.

  2. Consumer Revocation after Inactivity: If a lease expires and the provider fails to settle within the 24-hour settlement grace window, the consumer can invoke revoke_expired_lease. This revokes the lease and refunds 100% of the locked deposit directly to the consumer. See Protocol: Exact grace-window boundaries and Security: Guarantees.

docs.title: Why does the 24-hour grace window exist, and who can settle during it?
docs.text:
The 24-hour grace window (SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS = 86_400) protects providers from losing earned compensation due to transient network latency, RPC restarts, or temporary downtime at the moment of lease expiry.

  • During the window (expires_at <= now < expires_at + 86_400): Only the provider can settle via settle_lease. The consumer cannot revoke during this period (RevokeWindowNotElapsed).
  • After the window (now >= expires_at + 86_400): The consumer gains the right to call revoke_expired_lease to reclaim 100% of their escrow if the provider has still not settled. See Protocol: The 24-hour grace window and Boundary tests.

docs.title: What happens if a consumer or provider loses their secret key?
docs.text:
• If the Consumer loses their secret key: Escrowed funds remain locked in the contract until the lease expires. If the provider is operational, the provider can still call settle_lease to receive its earned payout; any remaining refund will be returned to the consumer's on-chain address (which the consumer cannot access without the lost key). If the provider never settles, the funds remain locked indefinitely, because only the consumer's key can sign revoke_expired_lease.
  • If the Provider loses their secret key: The provider cannot authorize settle_lease, forfeiting its ability to claim payouts for delivered calls. Once the lease duration and the 24-hour grace window elapse (now >= expires_at + 86_400), the consumer can invoke revoke_expired_lease using their own key to reclaim 100% of the escrowed funds. See Security: Trust assumptions and Guarantees.

docs.title: Which tokens are supported, and can the escrow token be changed?
docs.text:
• Supported Tokens: KeyLease supports any asset implementing the Soroban SEP-41 token interface. This includes the native Stellar Asset Contract (SAC) for XLM, classic wrapped assets (like USDC), and custom Soroban token contracts.
  • Changing the Token: The admin can configure or update the token address via set_token(admin, new_token_address). Existing, in-flight leases are settled in the token asset that was locked when they were created; newly created leases will use the updated token address. See Networks: Native SAC vs. Custom SEP-41 Token and Contract reference: set_token.

docs.title: What happens when the Stellar Testnet resets?
docs.text: Stellar Testnet resets occur 2–4 times per year to clean up ledger storage. When a reset occurs: 1. All ledger entries—including deployed contract bytecodes, contract instances, services, and leases—are completely wiped. 2. The contract ID and service IDs cease to exist. 3. Operators must re-run the deployment script (./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh) to deploy a fresh registry instance, re-initialize the admin and token, and re-register services. 4. Clients and providers must update their environment configurations with the new KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID. See Networks: Testnet resets and Deployment.

docs.title: Integration
docs.text:
KeyLease has no privileged off-chain service and no bespoke credential format. A provider integrates with the Stellar ledger directly: it verifies the lease on chain, binds the caller to the lease's consumer using Stellar account authentication, and settles through the contract.

This page describes the supported pattern. Any implementation that follows it is compatible with the protocol.

docs.title: What the credential is
docs.text:
The lease is the credential. get_lease(lease_id) returns the authoritative terms: allocated_calls, used_calls, expires_at, settled, and the consumer who owns the refund path. A provider admits a request only when that on-chain record says it is allowed.

There is nothing else to issue: no API key, no session JWT, no signing secret. The consumer's identity is its Stellar address (G… or C…).

docs.title: The verification pipeline
docs.text:
A provider should implement these steps, in order, and fail closed at every one:

  1. Authenticate the caller with Stellar. Use a challenge–response flow with the consumer's Stellar key; SEP-10 Stellar Web Authentication is the standard way to prove account ownership to an off-chain service. The result is a trusted Address for the request — not a password.
  2. Resolve the lease on chain. Call get_lease(lease_id) over Soroban RPC and cache the result briefly (a few seconds is usually enough for a busy provider). An unreachable RPC is a 503, never an allow.
  3. Check the lease. The lease must exist, must not be settled, and ledger.timestamp() < expires_at. Reject otherwise (403).
  4. Check ownership. The authenticated address must equal lease.consumer. Otherwise reject (403). This is what makes a stolen lease id worthless.
  5. Enforce the quota. Use max(lease.used_calls, local_counter) against lease.allocated_calls; reject with 429 when exhausted, and increment the counter only for admitted requests.
  6. Serve the request, adding the remaining-calls header if you want the client to see its budget.
  7. Settle with settle_lease when the lease expires or when the allotment is fully consumed.

Step 5's local counter is an optimisation, not the source of truth. On-chain allocated_calls × rate_per_call bounds what the provider can ever be paid, so a tampered counter can only make the provider charge less. It can never over-charge the consumer.

docs.title: Reading a lease
docs.text:
With the Stellar CLI:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet -- get_lease --lease_id 1

With @stellar/stellar-sdk, simulate a get_lease invocation and decode the result:

import {
  Contract, TransactionBuilder, Networks, Account,
  nativeToScVal, scValToNative, rpc,
} from '@stellar/stellar-sdk';

const server = new rpc.Server(process.env.KEYLEASE_RPC_URL!);
const contract = new Contract(process.env.KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID!);

export async function readLease(leaseId: bigint) {
  const source = new Account(
    'GAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAWHF',
    '0',
  );
  const tx = new TransactionBuilder(source, {
    fee: '100',
    networkPassphrase: Networks.TESTNET,
  })
    .addOperation(contract.call('get_lease', nativeToScVal(leaseId, { type: 'u64' })))
    .setTimeout(30)
    .build();

  const sim = await server.simulateTransaction(tx);
  if (!rpc.Api.isSimulationSuccess(sim) || !sim.result) {
    throw new Error('get_lease failed');
  }
  return scValToNative(sim.result.retval) as {
    lease_id: bigint;
    service_id: bigint;
    consumer: string;
    allocated_calls: number;
    used_calls: number;
    expires_at: bigint;
    locked_deposit: bigint;
    settled: boolean;
  };
}

The read views require no authorization, so simulation is enough — a provider never needs a Stellar secret key to verify a lease. That is deliberate: compromising an enforcement tier does not compromise escrowed funds.

docs.title: Following the event stream
docs.text:
For accounting, dashboards and settlement automation, subscribe to the contract's events instead of polling every lease:

stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger>

An event's first topic is always the event name as a symbol; the fields marked #[topic] in contracts/registry/src/events.rs follow it, and every remaining field is carried in the payload map. Topics are what a subscriber filters on, so which side of that line a field falls on decides whether you can act on it without decoding.

docs.title: Topics, payloads and filters
docs.text:
The --topic filter takes base64-encoded ScVal segments, one per topic position, and matches only events with exactly that many topics unless the last segment is the ** wildcard. A * segment matches any single topic.

Event Topics (in order) Payload-only fields Filter lease_created name, lease_id service_id, consumer, allocated_calls, expires_at, locked_deposit --topic "AAAADwAAAA1sZWFzZV9jcmVhdGVkAAAA,*" lease_settled name, lease_id provider, verified_calls, payout, refund --topic "AAAADwAAAA1sZWFzZV9zZXR0bGVkAAAA,*" lease_revoked name, lease_id consumer, refund --topic "AAAADwAAAA1sZWFzZV9yZXZva2VkAAAA,*" service_registered name, service_id provider, rate_per_call, endpoint_hash --topic "AAAADwAAABJzZXJ2aWNlX3JlZ2lzdGVyZWQAAA==,*" service_status_changed name, service_id provider, is_active --topic "AAAADwAAABZzZXJ2aWNlX3N0YXR1c19jaGFuZ2VkAAA=,*" contract_upgraded name only admin, new_wasm_hash --topic "AAAADwAAABFjb250cmFjdF91cGdyYWRlZAAAAA==" registry_initialized name only admin --topic "AAAADwAAABRyZWdpc3RyeV9pbml0aWFsaXplZA==" escrow_token_set name only admin, token --topic "AAAADwAAABBlc2Nyb3dfdG9rZW5fc2V0"

Note that only five of the eight events carry an id topic at all: contract_upgraded, registry_initialized and escrow_token_set have no id topics, so they can only be narrowed by contract id, and a lease's service_id is payload-only — a per-service queue must decode the payload rather than filter. Regenerate any of these strings yourself when you need a different id, e.g. for lease 1:

printf '{"symbol":"lease_created"}' | stellar xdr encode --type ScVal
# AAAADwAAAA1sZWFzZV9jcmVhdGVkAAAA
printf '{"u64":"1"}' | stellar xdr encode --type ScVal
# AAAABQAAAAAAAAAB
stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger> \
  --topic "AAAADwAAAA1sZWFzZV9jcmVhdGVkAAAA,AAAABQAAAAAAAAAB"

--output json and --output pretty decode names and fields for you, which is usually enough for a one-off check; the encoded filters matter when a subscriber needs the server to narrow the stream.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text:
• lease_created — open (or upsert) a lease record keyed by lease_id, storing service_id, consumer, allocated_calls, expires_at and locked_deposit from the payload, and push it onto the settlement queue ordered by expires_at. This is the only event that tells you escrow exists, so anything you do not record here must be re-read with get_lease.
  • lease_settled — close the lease in your ledger and reconcile: assert payout + refund == locked_deposit from the create event, and credit the provider payout. A payout of 0 means the provider refunded a lease it could not serve, which is worth alerting on.
  • lease_revoked — mark the lease closed with no revenue and record it against the provider's reliability. refund here is always the full locked_deposit. This event is also the only way to tell a revocation apart from a zero-call settlement, because both leave settled = true: see LeaseStatus and the settled flag.
  • service_status_changed — update the catalogue entry for service_id. is_active = false blocks new create_lease calls only, so stop quoting the service to new consumers while still serving and settling leases you already hold.
  • contract_upgraded — the running logic changed. Take new_wasm_hash from the payload, confirm version() reports the release you expected, and re-run the post-upgrade checks in Upgrading before trusting new leases. Reconcile any in-flight lease counters your indexer holds, because the payload carries no ids to scope this to.
  • service_registered — add the service to the catalogue with its rate_per_call and endpoint_hash; the hash is the commitment your enforcement layer compares the real endpoint against.
  • registry_initialized / escrow_token_set — deployment-lifecycle events. Treat escrow_token_set as a hard stop: the escrow asset changed, so the unit of every payout and refund you have been accumulating changed with it.

Every id you can filter on is in the table above; event names, topics and payload fields are part of the ABI and are listed in the contract reference.

docs.title: Event schema version
docs.text:
Every payload includes a schema_version key (u32), and the contract also publishes it as on-chain metadata under eventSchemaVersion. The number describes the event schema, not the release: version moves on every deploy, schema_version only when an event gains or loses a field. Fields are added and never removed, renamed or retyped, and topics never change, so an old decoder keeps working on new events.

Branch on the payload key, not on the contract's version:

Payload says What to do no schema_version key Revision 0: an event from before versioning was introduced. Its fields are today's fields minus schema_version, so decode it with the current parser and ignore the missing key. 0 < schema_version <= 1 Decode the keys you know and ignore any extra key. A payload newer than your build within the same major revision stays readable by design. schema_version > 1 Your decoder is behind the deployment. Store the event verbatim, surface it as unhandled, and alert — do not guess at the shape of an escrow record. 
version = payload.get("schema_version", 0)   # absent means pre-versioning
if version > SUPPORTED_SCHEMA_VERSION:
    quarantine(event)                        # never silently drop escrow

Prefer the payload key over the eventSchemaVersion metadata when decoding history: metadata describes the Wasm running now, while an event from an old ledger was emitted by the schema that was running then. Read the metadata once at startup to learn the current version, and index from there.

docs.title: Storage lifetime
docs.text:
Lease and service entries are persistent entries with a bounded lifetime, and reading one no longer extends it. If you keep a long-lived projection of leases, you may want to keep the on-chain record alive alongside it:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account indexer --network testnet \
  -- bump_lease --lease_id 1

bump_lease and bump_service are permissionless; whoever calls them pays the rent for the extension. A bump can only lengthen a lifetime, never shorten it, and bump_lease rejects a settled lease, so there is nothing to grief with an entry whose funds have already moved. Settlement itself and create_lease keep the entries they touch alive on their own; you only need an explicit bump for state that is being read and not written for the length of its horizon.

docs.title: Settling
docs.text:
Settlement is one signed transaction from the provider account, at or after expiry, or as soon as every allocated call is consumed:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- settle_lease \
    --provider $PROVIDER --lease_id 1 --verified_calls 320

Reporting verified_calls = 0 refunds the entire deposit for a lease you could not serve. Choose a settlement cadence that fits your traffic: one settlement per lease, not per request.

docs.title: Hardening checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Verify leases server-side; never trust a lease_id supplied by the client without checking consumer against an authenticated Stellar address.
  • [ ] Fail closed on RPC errors, malformed lease data and unknown leases.
  • [ ] Cache lease reads briefly (≈5–30 s) but never past the request you are authorising; re-read on a cache miss or when close to expires_at.
  • [ ] Share the per-lease counter if you run more than one instance, or accept that each instance can grant the full allotment (the provider only loses revenue; the consumer is still bounded on chain).
  • [ ] Keep provider signing keys out of the request path where possible: reads need no key, only settlement does.
  • [ ] Watch lease_created so no lease expires unsettled and becomes revocable.
  • [ ] Never log Stellar secret seeds.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Every API and RPC provider on Stellar hands out the same artifact: a static API key. That credential is a liability on both sides of the relationship.

For developers, it is a secret that lives forever in a .env file. It leaks through committed repositories, CI logs, screenshots and shared machines, and because it never expires, a leak is a permanent leak. Rotating it breaks every consumer at once.

For providers, a static key means an all-or-nothing relationship. You cannot sell 1,000 calls to someone; you either grant unlimited access, or you build and operate your own billing, quota and revocation infrastructure. Usage cannot be metered on-chain, so nobody can prove what was consumed.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
KeyLease turns metered access into a lease, and puts the lease on Stellar.

A consumer locks a SEP-41 micropayment in Soroban escrow and receives an on-chain authorization for a fixed allotment of calls. The provider verifies the lease against Stellar instead of trusting a password, settles once with a verified call count, and is paid from escrow. Unused balance refunds automatically.

consumer                         registry                        provider
   |                                |                                |
   |-- create_lease(calls, secs) -->|                                |
   |   (escrow = rate * calls)      |                                |
   |<-- lease_id ------------------ |                                |
   |                                |                                |
   |                                |<-- settle_lease(used_calls) ---|
   |<-- refund of unused ---------- |---- payout of used ----------->|
   |                                |                                |

Two properties fall out of this design that a static key cannot offer:

  1. The credential expires on its own. Authorization is bounded by expires_at, read from ledger time. There is nothing to rotate and nothing to leak permanently.
  2. Nobody can strand your money. If the provider never settles, the consumer reclaims the entire deposit 24 hours after expiry. That refund path is what makes escrow safe to use against a provider you have never met.

docs.title: Why this is a Stellar protocol
docs.text:
KeyLease is not an off-chain SaaS that happens to store a hash on a chain. The ledger is the system of record and each part of the design maps to a Stellar primitive:

Requirement Stellar primitive Hold and move the payment SEP-41 token; the native Stellar Asset Contract (SAC) wraps XLM Prove who created or settled a lease Address authorization; accounts (G…) and contracts (C…) both work, including Stellar multisig Know when a lease expires Ledger timestamp, not an operator's clock Prove what happened Typed Soroban contract events (lease_created, lease_settled, …) Keep escrow claimable Persistent-storage TTL, extended for the lease's term + grace window on every state change and by the permissionless bump_lease Identify the deployed code contractmeta! (name, version, description, repository) and version() Fix a deployed bug propose_upgrade → 24h delay → execute_upgrade through the Soroban deployer

The consumer's proof of access is the lease itself. A provider reads it from Soroban RPC (or follows the event stream) and binds the caller to the lease's consumer address using Stellar signatures — no second credential format is invented. See Integration.

docs.title: What KeyLease is not
docs.text:
• Not a payment processor. It moves a SEP-41 token between a consumer, a provider, and escrow. It does not touch fiat.
  • Not an HTTP service. The contract cannot see your traffic. Quota checking and request forwarding are the provider's job; the on-chain lease bounds what any implementation may charge.
  • Not a credential store. Providers publish endpoint_hash, a commitment to their off-chain endpoint descriptor. No secret is ever written on-chain.

docs.title: Where it fits in the Stellar ecosystem
docs.text:
Stellar's Soroban runtime makes this practical: sub-cent fees, ~5 second ledger close, and native SEP-41 tokens mean a lease can be created, settled and refunded cheaply enough to be worth doing for small allotments of calls.

KeyLease targets a specific gap: metered API/RPC credential leasing. Adjacent Stellar escrow projects focus on milestone-based work and P2P rental escrow. Metered access — a fixed number of calls that expires — is the white space this protocol occupies.

docs.title: Escrow asset: the native SAC
docs.text:
On Testnet the usual escrow asset is the native Stellar Asset Contract for XLM. Its address is derived from the network passphrase, not invented:

stellar contract id asset --network testnet --asset native

Any SEP-41 token can be configured instead with set_token; the derive command above is only for the native asset. The admin must call set_token before any lease can be created (TokenNotSet otherwise).

docs.title: Native SAC vs. Custom SEP-41 Token
docs.text:
KeyLease accepts any contract implementing the SEP-41 token standard. Operators evaluating which asset to configure should consider the architectural and operational trade-offs:

Characteristic Native SAC (XLM) Custom SEP-41 Token / Classic SAC Issuance Native protocol asset built into the Stellar consensus layer Minted by an issuer account (classic asset wrapper) or custom token contract Trustlines None required; every funded Stellar account natively holds XLM Classic assets require explicit trustlines (ChangeTrust); contract-native tokens manage balances internally Decimals Fixed at 7 decimals (1 stroop = 0.0000001 XLM) Configurable (commonly 7 for classic wrapped assets, 6 for USDC, or 18 for EVM-style tokens) Admin controls None. No freeze, no clawback, no issuer key, no upgradeability Issuer may configure clawback, authorization flags (auth_required), pausing, or contract upgradeability Escrow guarantees Escrow lock and transfer are guaranteed by host runtime; zero re-entrancy or transfer-failure risk Follows identical SEP-41 contract interface, but subject to issuer freeze, clawback, or contract bugs

docs.title: Escrow guarantees and risk profile
docs.text:
From KeyLease's perspective, both token types interact through the same standard interface (token::Client). Escrow invariants (payout + refund == locked_deposit) hold equally across both.

However, external contract risk differs: - Native SAC: The transfer cannot be blocked, paused, or redirected by any third party. - Custom Token: If a custom token contract fails, pauses, or blacklists a participant, calls to settle_lease or revoke_expired_lease will revert. KeyLease uses checks-effects-interactions (lease.settled = true persisted before transfer) to prevent double-spend or re-entrancy attacks, but cannot force a failing external token to execute transfers.

docs.title: Deployment recommendations
docs.text:
• Testnet: Use the Native SAC (XLM). It requires zero setup, is automatically derived from the network passphrase, and accounts can be funded immediately via Friendbot.
  • Mainnet: Use USDC via SAC for commercial API and RPC leases where price volatility between fiat costs and crypto balances is undesirable. Use Native SAC (XLM) for network infrastructure services, peer-to-peer compute, or micro-metered telemetry where native settlement is preferred.

docs.title: Funding accounts
docs.text:
Friendbot funds accounts and contracts with 10,000 fake XLM on Testnet:

stellar keys generate consumer --network testnet --fund
# or, for an address you already have:
curl "https://friendbot.stellar.org?addr=$(stellar keys address consumer)"

The CLI's --fund flag and the HTTP endpoint above are for networks with a friendbot: Testnet, and the local container's own friendbot at http://localhost:8000/friendbot (stellar keys generate x --network local --fund hits it). Mainnet has neither and requires real XLM for fees and for the escrowed asset. See Developer guide → Local sandbox walkthrough.

docs.title: Testnet resets
docs.text:
Testnet resets wipe all ledger entries, including the deployed contract, services and leases, 2–4 times per year at 17:00 UTC.

After a reset, the contract id changes. Re-run scripts/deploy-testnet.sh and update docs/deployments.md.

docs.title: What a reset actually takes
docs.text:
A reset is not a data purge of the deployment — it is a purge of the whole ledger, so plan for these to be gone:

Gone Survives The registry contract instance, its Wasm reference and its contractmeta!. Your local Stellar CLI identities. Seeds are stored on your machine, so KEYLEASE_ADMIN / KEYLEASE_PROVIDER / KEYLEASE_CONSUMER keep the same G… addresses. All instance storage: Admin, Token, ServiceCount, LeaseCount. The native SAC address. It is derived from the network passphrase, which a reset does not change — re-derive it with stellar contract id asset --network testnet --asset native and expect the same value. All persistent storage: every Service(id) and Lease(id) entry. The repository, its CI, and your built Wasm. Every funded account, including the SAC balances and any open lease's escrow. Nothing on-chain that identifies your old deployment.

Open leases are the expensive part: their Lease entries, and therefore their refund paths, are gone. Testnet escrow is fake XLM, so the loss is nuisance rather than damage, but any indexer or provider middleware that caches lease state has to be rewound too.

docs.title: After a Testnet reset
docs.text:
Redeploy in dependency order — the same order scripts/deploy-testnet.sh enforces, because each step reads what the previous one wrote.

cd keylease-core && git fetch origin && git switch main && git pull --ff-only

# 1. Re-create and re-fund the signing identity (Friendbot creates the account
#    if it is missing; the address is the same as before the reset).
stellar keys generate keylease-admin --network testnet --fund
#    Reusing an existing seed instead of generating one:
curl "https://friendbot.stellar.org?addr=$(stellar keys address keylease-admin)"

# 2. Build, deploy, init, set_token and register_service in one pass.
SOURCE_ACCOUNT=keylease-admin ./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh

The script's steps 2–5 are the redeploy, re-init, token-set and re-register steps. Run them individually only if you need to interpose something:

REGISTRY=$(stellar contract deploy \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet | tail -n1)

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- init --admin "$(stellar keys address keylease-admin)"

TOKEN=$(stellar contract id asset --network testnet --asset native)
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- set_token \
     --admin "$(stellar keys address keylease-admin)" --token "$TOKEN"

stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- register_service \
     --provider "$(stellar keys address keylease-admin)" \
     --rate_per_call 1000000 --endpoint_hash <64_HEX_CHARS>

register_service returns 1 again. That is expected, not a collision: ServiceCount lived in instance storage, and the instance is new. Lease ids restart the same way. Consumers holding a service_id from before the reset must re-read it from Deployments or from the script output.

docs.title: After a reset: update the record and the config
docs.text:
1. .env — copy the values the script prints. The three that change every reset are KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID, KEYLEASE_SERVICE_ID and, if you rebuilt, nothing else; KEYLEASE_TOKEN_ADDRESS, KEYLEASE_NETWORK, KEYLEASE_RPC_URL and the account addresses do not change. Restart anything that reads the file — clients pick the contract id up at construction.
  2. docs/deployments.md — replace the Testnet row's KeyLeaseRegistry id, contract version, Wasm hash, the Contract created ledger and the four tx links for init / set_token / register_service. Leave the "Escrow token (native SAC)" row alone unless you switched assets. Follow Recording a deployment, and tag the revision so a reader can tie the new ids to a commit.
  3. Cursors — an indexer following the old contract id has nothing to read and will not error loudly. Point it at the new id and start it at the deployment ledger; see Integration.

docs.title: Check the old contract id is dead
docs.text:
Do this before announcing the new id, so a stale pointer cannot be mistaken for a working one. Both commands must fail, because no ledger entry backs the old id:

OLD=CCEZYHUJUICXVPLH6UC2OFZL2RG23QQ7EMZOWE32WVQPT25DCTIAFH62   # from git history

stellar contract info fetch --id "$OLD" --network testnet
stellar contract invoke --id "$OLD" --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet -- version
stellar events --id "$OLD" --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger just after the reset>

info fetch reports the entry is missing and the invoke fails during simulation — there is no instance to load. stellar events answers with an empty list, not an error: absence of history is the same fact stated quietly.

If version() answers, you are not looking at a reset network. Either the reset has not happened yet, or the RPC you are pointing at is a different network — check stellar network ls and the passphrase above before publishing anything.

docs.title: Explorer links
docs.text:
Each network has a contract explorer. Substitute the id from Deployments:

Network Contract URL Testnet https://stellar.expert/explorer/testnet/contract/<CONTRACT_ID> Mainnet https://stellar.expert/explorer/public/contract/<CONTRACT_ID>

docs.title: RPC production notes
docs.text:
• Testnet and Futurenet public RPCs are rate-limited. They are fine for demos and reads, not for a busy provider.
  • For production, use an authenticated RPC provider and pass its URL through KEYLEASE_RPC_URL.
  • A provider's verification path fails closed when RPC is unreachable: it must reject requests rather than admit unverified ones. No funds move either way, and settlement/revocation remain possible directly through the contract.

docs.text:

  • Integration — how to read leases and events from a service.

docs.title: Actors
docs.text:
Actor Address Can do Admin one Stellar account init once, set_token, propose_upgrade/execute_upgrade/cancel_upgrade (24h delay). Cannot move escrowed funds. Provider per service (account or contract address) Register/pause services, settle leases it owns. Consumer per lease (account or contract address) Create leases, revoke expired unsettled leases.

The admin is a deployment role. It can point the registry at a token address and install a new Wasm, and nothing else. It has no path to user funds.

Because every actor is a Soroban Address, the same protocol works for classic Stellar accounts (G…), multisig accounts and smart contracts (C…).

docs.title: Service
docs.text:
pub struct Service {
    pub service_id: u64,
    pub provider: Address,
    pub rate_per_call: i128,   // smallest unit of the escrow token
    pub is_active: bool,
    pub endpoint_hash: BytesN<32>,
}

A service is not an endpoint URL and not a credential. It is a price and a commitment. endpoint_hash is a 32-byte digest of the provider's off-chain descriptor, so the on-chain record proves what the endpoint should be without publishing anything secret.

docs.title: Lease
docs.text:
pub struct Lease {
    pub lease_id: u64,
    pub service_id: u64,
    pub consumer: Address,
    pub allocated_calls: u32,
    pub used_calls: u32,
    pub expires_at: u64,       // unix seconds, ledger time
    pub locked_deposit: i128,  // rate_per_call * allocated_calls
    pub settled: bool,
}

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Active: create_lease<br/>(escrow rate × calls)
    Active --> Expired: now ≥ expires_at
    Active --> Settled: settle_lease<br/>(verified_calls == allocated_calls)
    Expired --> Settled: settle_lease<br/>(provider, within grace)
    Expired --> Settled: revoke_expired_lease<br/>(consumer, after 24h grace)
    Settled --> [*]

lease_status derives the state from settled and expires_at:

Status Discriminant Condition Active 0 not settled, now < expires_at Expired 1 not settled, now ≥ expires_at Settled 2 settled == true

Discriminants are stable on the wire. They will never be renumbered.

docs.title: Settled is one state, reached two ways
docs.text:
settled records that escrow has left the contract — it does not record why. Both terminal transitions set it: settle_lease after paying the provider, and revoke_expired_lease after refunding the consumer in full. So Settled is the answer to "is this lease finished?", never to "did the provider earn?", and Error::LeaseAlreadySettled (7) likewise means "already settled or revoked".

The two paths are separable, but not from the status:

  • used_calls is written only by settle_lease, so settled && used_calls > 0 is a provider settlement.
  • settled && used_calls == 0 is ambiguous: a revocation, or a settlement reported with verified_calls = 0, which is the provider's legitimate way of refunding a lease it could not serve. The two leave identical storage.
  • The published event is the only discriminator — lease_settled versus lease_revoked for that lease_id.
Lifecycle event settled used_calls lease_status create_lease false 0 Active settle_lease(320) of 500, after expiry true 320 Settled settle_lease(0) of 500, after expiry true 0 Settled revoke_expired_lease after the grace window true 0 Settled

The full state-by-event table, including remaining_calls and locked_balance, is in LeaseStatus and the settled flag, and how to consume the two events is in Following the event stream.

docs.title: When can a lease be settled?
docs.text:
settle_lease reverts with LeaseNotSettleable unless either:

  • the lease has expired (now ≥ expires_at), or
  • verified_calls == allocated_calls.

The second clause is the "consumer got what it paid for" fast path: if every allocated call was consumed, the provider should not have to wait for expiry to be paid.

docs.title: The 24-hour grace window
docs.text:
After expiry there is a 24-hour window (SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS = 86_400) during which only the provider can settle. Once it elapses, the consumer may call revoke_expired_lease and reclaim the entire deposit.

expires_at ────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┬──────────────▶ time
                               │                             │
                        expiry reached              expires_at + 24h
                               │                             │
        provider may settle for the whole window    consumer may revoke
                               │                             │
                        ───────┴──── provider grace ─────────┘

Why a grace window at all? Without it, a provider that was offline for a minute at expiry would lose a legitimate payout to a consumer racing to revoke. The window gives providers a guaranteed settlement period while keeping the consumer's exit bounded at 24 hours.

docs.title: Exact grace-window boundaries
docs.text:
The contract evaluates time against ledger timestamp (env.ledger().timestamp()). The exact inclusive and exclusive boundary conditions are:

Condition / Interval Status (lease_status) settle_lease (Provider) revoke_expired_lease (Consumer) Allowed Transitions now < expires_at Active (0) Allowed only if verified_calls == allocated_calls; otherwise reverts (LeaseNotSettleable) Reverts (LeaseNotExpired) Early full-consumption settlement only now == expires_at Expired (1) Allowed for any verified_calls <= allocated_calls Reverts (RevokeWindowNotElapsed) Provider settlement begins expires_at <= now < expires_at + 86_400 Expired (1) Allowed for any verified_calls <= allocated_calls Reverts (RevokeWindowNotElapsed) Exclusive provider settlement window now >= expires_at + 86_400 Expired (1) Allowed if not yet revoked; reverts (LeaseAlreadySettled) once revoked Allowed; refunds 100% of locked deposit to consumer Consumer revocation enabled (first revocable second is expires_at + 86_400)

docs.title: Boundary verification tests
docs.text:
These boundary conditions are unit-tested and asserted in contracts/registry/src/test.rs:

  • test_revoke_before_expiry_is_rejected: verifies that when now < expires_at, revoke_expired_lease returns Err(Error::LeaseNotExpired).
  • test_full_usage_can_settle_before_expiry: confirms early settlement when verified_calls == allocated_calls even when now < expires_at.
  • test_provider_can_settle_within_grace_window: confirms provider payout at expires_at + GRACE / 2 (12 hours into grace).
  • test_revoke_during_grace_window_is_rejected: asserts revoke_expired_lease reverts with Err(Error::RevokeWindowNotElapsed) at expires_at + GRACE - 1 (the final second of provider grace).
  • test_expired_unsettled_lease_is_fully_reclaimed: verifies consumer revocation succeeds at exactly expires_at + GRACE, returning 100% of escrowed deposit.
  • test_lease_ttl_ask_floors_once_the_grace_window_is_past: ensures storage rent bumps clamp gracefully after the grace period has elapsed.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Every transition publishes a typed Soroban event. Event names are the first topic, followed by the id fields marked #[topic]; the payload is a map of the remaining fields. Each payload also carries schema_version, so a stream that spans a contract upgrade stays decodable (see Integration → Event schema version).

Event Topics Data registry_initialized — schema_version, admin escrow_token_set — schema_version, admin, token service_registered service_id schema_version, provider, rate_per_call, endpoint_hash service_status_changed service_id schema_version, provider, is_active lease_created lease_id schema_version, service_id, consumer, allocated_calls, expires_at, locked_deposit lease_settled lease_id schema_version, provider, verified_calls, payout, refund lease_revoked lease_id schema_version, consumer, refund contract_upgraded — schema_version, admin, new_wasm_hash

Events are the indexing contract between on-chain state and off-chain systems: a provider can settle from a projection built by subscribing to lease_created, and accounting can reconcile payouts from lease_settled without polling every lease. See Integration.

docs.title: Worked economics
docs.text:
All figures use the escrow token's smallest unit (7 decimals for the native asset, so 1 XLM = 10_000_000).

Suppose a provider registers a service at rate_per_call = 1_000_000 (0.1 XLM per call), and a consumer buys 500 calls for 1 hour.

1. create_lease

required_deposit = rate_per_call × requested_calls
                 = 1_000_000 × 500
                 = 500_000_000        (50 XLM)

The registry transfers 500_000_000 from the consumer into escrow and sets expires_at = now + 3600.

2a. settle_lease after 1 hour with 320 calls consumed

payout = 1_000_000 × 320 = 320_000_000   (32 XLM to the provider)
refund = 500_000_000 − 320_000_000
       = 180_000_000                     (18 XLM back to the consumer)

2b. Provider goes dark; consumer calls revoke_expired_lease after 24h

refund = locked_deposit = 500_000_000    (50 XLM, the full deposit)

2c. Consumer burns all 500 calls in 10 minutes

settle_lease is immediately allowed (verified_calls == allocated_calls):

payout = 1_000_000 × 500 = 500_000_000   (50 XLM)
refund = 0

docs.title: Cost of the lease itself
docs.text:
Creating a lease costs one Soroban transaction (fees plus the escrow transfer). Settlement costs one more. There is no per-call on-chain cost — the provider settles with a single call count, which is what makes this cheap enough for small allotments.

The create transaction also pays Soroban storage rent for extending the lease entry through its term, the 24-hour grace window and a one-day buffer. Rent scales with the duration and the number of entries, not with the number of calls, so short leases stay cheap and the TTL is deliberately not padded to the thirty-day default.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
These must hold for every reachable state. They are asserted in tests.

  1. Conservation. For every lease, payout + refund == locked_deposit.
  2. Single release. A settled lease can never be settled or revoked again (LeaseAlreadySettled), and settled is persisted before any token call.
  3. Bounded claim. A provider can never receive more than allocated_calls × rate_per_call, and only for a service it owns.
  4. Guaranteed exit. Every lease has a consumer path to a full refund.
  5. Checked math. Deposit, payout and timestamp arithmetic abort on overflow rather than truncating.
  6. Claimable storage. A lease's persistent entry outlives its term plus the grace window (MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS = 30 days).

docs.title: Storage and lifetime
docs.text:
Key Storage Notes Admin, Token instance configuration; instance TTL is bumped on every state change ServiceCount, LeaseCount instance monotonic id counters Service(u64) persistent TTL extended on save and by bump_service Lease(u64) persistent TTL extended on save and by bump_lease, never by a read

LEDGER_BUMP_THRESHOLD = 17_280 ledgers (~1 day at 5s ledgers) and LEDGER_BUMP_EXTEND = 518_400 ledgers (~30 days). For leases, save_lease and bump_lease extend to (expires_at − now + 24h) / 5s + LEDGER_BUMP_THRESHOLD ledgers, so the escrow stays claimable for the whole lease, the provider's grace window and a one-day read buffer — without paying rent for unused storage time. Once a lease is past its term and grace window that ask settles at about two days, so keeping a dead lease alive costs rent per bump rather than per month.

Rent scales with that ask: at the ledger where an extension is due, bump_lease estimates 48,684 stroops of persistent rent for a 30-day-term lease against zero for get_lease, which is why reads do not extend. MAX_ENTRY_TTL_LEDGERS (1,555,200 ledgers ≈ 90 days) caps any single extension, and the cap is also taken against the network's live maxEntryTtl, so an entry's horizon is never derived from stored expires_at alone.

docs.title: Provider guide
docs.text: You run an API or RPC endpoint. This guide shows how to sell metered access to it with KeyLease instead of handing out a static key, using only Stellar tooling and the Soroban contract.

docs.title: What you are agreeing to
docs.text:
• You publish a price per call and a 32-byte endpoint_hash commitment.
  • Consumers escrow price × calls in a SEP-41 token before they can make a request.
  • You settle a lease once, reporting how many calls were consumed.
  • If you never settle, the consumer reclaims the full deposit 24 hours after expiry. That guarantee is what makes consumers willing to prepay.

You never publish a secret on-chain. endpoint_hash is a commitment, not a credential.

docs.title: 1. Register a service
docs.text:
export REGISTRY=<your registry contract id>
export PROVIDER=$(stellar keys address provider)

stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- register_service \
     --provider $PROVIDER \
     --rate_per_call 1000000 \
     --endpoint_hash $(printf '%s' "$PROVIDER:my-api" | sha256sum | awk '{print $1}')

rate_per_call is in the escrow token's smallest unit (7 decimals for the native asset, so 1000000 = 0.1 XLM per call). The command prints the new service_id — record it.

register_service accepts any positive rate, but MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT caps the product: at your rate, the largest lease a consumer can open is MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT ÷ rate_per_call calls. A rate of 1000000 leaves room for 1,000,000 calls; a rate of 100000000 caps them at 10,000. Price the whole allotment your typical customer wants before you pick one.

The registration emits service_registered { service_id, provider, rate_per_call, endpoint_hash }, so your own indexer can pick it up without a separate query.

docs.title: 2. Pause or resume a service
docs.text:
stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- set_service_active --provider $PROVIDER --service_id 1 --is_active false

Deactivation blocks new leases only. Existing leases stay valid and must still be settleable — you remain obligated to settle or let them expire. The change emits service_status_changed.

docs.title: 3. Verify leases and meter calls
docs.text: The contract cannot see your HTTP traffic, so verification and metering happen in your request path. The credential is the on-chain lease; there is no session token to mint.

docs.title: Verify against Soroban RPC
docs.text:
1. Authenticate the caller as a Stellar address (SEP-10 challenge–response is the standard approach).
  2. Read the lease with get_lease(lease_id) over Soroban RPC and cache it briefly.
  3. Reject if settled, if now ≥ expires_at, if the caller is not lease.consumer, or if your counter has consumed allocated_calls.
  4. Count the call, return the response.
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider \
  --network testnet -- get_lease --lease_id 1

Reads need no secret key: a verifier can run without any signing authority.

docs.title: Or project the event stream
docs.text:
If you would rather not call RPC per request, subscribe to lease_created and keep a local table of active leases. The on-chain allocated_calls and expires_at remain the bound; your projection is an optimisation.

The full pipeline, including the Stellar SDK read example and cache guidance, is in Integration.

docs.title: 4. Settle
docs.text:
Settle when the lease expires, or immediately once the consumer has used every allocated call. One settlement covers the whole lease — never one per request.

stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- settle_lease --provider $PROVIDER --lease_id 1 --verified_calls 320

The registry pays you verified_calls × rate_per_call, refunds the rest to the consumer, and emits lease_settled { lease_id, provider, verified_calls, payout, refund }.

Settle with verified_calls = 0 to return the entire deposit for a lease you could not serve.

docs.title: Settling rules
docs.text: Situation Result now ≥ expires_at, any verified_calls ≤ allocated_calls settle allowed verified_calls == allocated_calls, any time settle allowed now < expires_at and verified_calls < allocated_calls LeaseNotSettleable verified_calls > allocated_calls InvalidCalls lease already settled LeaseAlreadySettled you don't own the service Unauthorized

docs.title: 5. Accounting
docs.text:
settle_lease pays you from escrow. Nothing else does. The registry never holds funds on your behalf after settlement, and there is no yield or custody to manage.

  • Revenue recognised: verified_calls × rate_per_call per settlement, published in the lease_settled event.
  • Unused consumer balance: refunded by you at settlement, or by the consumer via revoke_expired_lease after the 24h grace window.
  • Disputes: there is no dispute mechanism. The consumer's protection is the refund path; yours is the grace window. Report honestly.

docs.title: Operational notes
docs.text:
• Watch expiry. A lease you forget to settle becomes revocable 24 hours after it expires. Subscribe to lease_created and settle from that queue.
  • Changing your rate. Today you register a new service; an update entry point is a wave-medium issue. In-flight leases keep their original escrow.
  • Rotating your key. A service is bound to the registering address; key rotation/transfer is a wave-medium issue. Register from an account you can keep — a Stellar multisig account works today.
  • Upgrades. Watch contract_upgraded and check version() after a release. Storage and balances are preserved across upgrades.
  • Testnet resets wipe your service. Re-register after each reset.
