docs.title: Security model
docs.text: KeyLease escrows funds on Stellar. This page states exactly what the Soroban contract guarantees, what it assumes, and what is not yet hardened. For reporting a vulnerability, see SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Trust assumptions
docs.text:
Assumption Consequence if violated The admin configures a well-behaved SEP-41 token. A malicious token contract could revert transfers and stall settlement. It cannot be paid twice: settled is persisted before the transfer, and a re-entrant token is rejected (LeaseAlreadySettled). The admin does not upgrade to a malicious Wasm. An upgrade can change the contract logic. The admin key should be cold or multisig. Upgrades now require a 24h on-ledger delay and emit upgrade_proposed with the hash and execution ledger, so consumers can exit; execution emits contract_upgraded. The provider reports verified_calls honestly. It can under-report (it gets paid less) but never over-report past allocated_calls. Soroban ledger time is monotonic and honest. Validity windows would be unreliable. Consumers keep their own key safe. Anyone with the consumer key can create leases that spend its balance.

The provider is explicitly untrusted in the direction that matters: it cannot take more than it is owed, and it cannot prevent the consumer's refund.

docs.title: Guarantees
docs.text:
1. The provider is paid at most allocated_calls × rate_per_call. The payout is computed from the stored rate_per_call and the lease allotment; an over-claim reverts with InvalidCalls.
  2. Only the owning provider can settle. settle_lease checks service.provider == provider after authenticating provider (Unauthorized).
  3. Only the consumer can revoke, and only after the grace window. Combined checks for ownership, expiry and elapsed grace (Unauthorized, LeaseNotExpired, RevokeWindowNotElapsed).
  4. A lease releases funds once. Every money path checks settled first, persists settled = true, and only then calls the token (LeaseAlreadySettled). Checks-effects-interactions is enforced by test_reentrant_token_cannot_settle_a_lease_twice.
  5. Overflow aborts. Deposit, payout and expiry arithmetic use checked_mul/checked_add/checked_sub and revert with Overflow.
  6. Lease durations are storage-safe. Durations above MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS (30 days) revert with DurationTooLong, and the persistent entry is extended for the term plus the grace window, so escrow cannot be evicted while it is claimable.
  7. A single lease cannot escrow an unbounded amount. A deposit that fits i128 but exceeds MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT reverts with DepositTooLarge, before the lease id is allocated and before the token is called. Checked arithmetic alone cannot catch this: a product can be perfectly representable and still be three orders of magnitude more than the consumer meant to lock.
  8. The admin cannot touch user funds. It can only call set_token and upgrade.
  9. Every mutation is authenticated. No state-changing entry point trusts its caller without require_auth().
  10. Every mutation is observable. Each transition emits a typed Soroban event with no secret material in it.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
Asserted in contracts/registry/src/test.rs. The contract reference lists the exact error code for each violation.

  • payout + refund == locked_deposit for every lease.
  • A settled lease never transitions again.
  • settled is true on-chain before any value leaves the contract.
  • No lease can leave more value than was escrowed.
  • Every lease has a consumer path to a full refund, for its entire TTL.

docs.title: Threats considered
docs.text: Threat Mitigation Provider claims more calls than allocated InvalidCalls Provider settles a lease twice settled flag persisted before transfers + LeaseAlreadySettled Attacker settles someone else's lease service.provider == provider check Attacker revokes someone else's lease lease.consumer == consumer check Re-entrant token pays a lease twice checks-effects-interactions; adversarial test Provider strands funds by never settling 24h grace, then full consumer refund Consumer races the provider at expiry 24h grace window reserved for the provider Rate overflow creates a cheap lease checked_mul → Overflow Typo locks a consumer into an enormous deposit MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT → DepositTooLarge Escrow token has more decimals than assumed MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT is in base units, so the ceiling tightens as the scale grows Duration overflow wraps expiry checked_add → Overflow Long lease is evicted from storage DurationTooLong + duration-aware TTL extension Fake "KeyLease" contract id Only ids in Deployments are ours Silent logic change on upgrade 24h delay + admin-only execution, emits upgrade_proposed/contract_upgraded, contractmeta! exposes the version

docs.title: Running with a multisig admin
docs.text: KeyLease stores the admin as a standard Soroban Address. In production, operators should avoid using a single hot keypair for the admin role. Instead, the admin can be a native Stellar multi-signature account (G...) or a multisig smart contract.

docs.title: Host-enforced authentication
docs.text: When admin.require_auth() is called inside set_token or upgrade: - If admin is a Stellar account, Soroban's runtime delegates authentication to Stellar's native account signing engine. - If the account is configured with multi-signature weights and operation thresholds (e.g., medium threshold for contract invocations), the Stellar host requires signatures that satisfy the threshold before the invocation transaction can execute. - The contract does not need special multisig code; multi-signature security is enforced natively at the protocol host layer.

docs.title: What the contract can and cannot enforce
docs.text: Scope Contract capability Details Can enforce Execution authority (require_auth) Ensures that the admin account legitimately approved the call based on Stellar's consensus rules Cannot enforce Signer composition The contract cannot inspect individual signers, public keys, or individual weights Cannot enforce Minimum threshold The contract cannot verify whether the admin account is 1-of-1, 2-of-3, or 3-of-5 Cannot enforce Signer set immutability Signers and thresholds can be modified on the Stellar account via standard SetOptions operations without contract interaction

docs.title: Audit status
docs.text: No external audit of this contract has been performed. As of v0.2.1 no third party has reviewed, formally verified or signed off on contracts/registry. No firm is engaged and no report exists. Everything on this page is the project's own claim about its own code: read Guarantees as a specification of what the authors intended, not as an independent finding.

docs.title: Coverage that exists
docs.text:
What How much Where Contract tests 63 contracts/registry/src/test.rs, run by cargo test --all Documented guarantees 10 Guarantees Invariants asserted in tests 5 Invariants Threats modelled 14 Threats considered CI gates 8 Format, Clippy, Test, Build (wasm32v1-none), Spell Check, Markdown Lint, Dependency Policy (cargo-deny) and Malware Scan (ClamAV) in .github/workflows/ci.yml

The counts are as of the revision this page is written against; each one is mechanically checkable from the file it names.

Two of the 63 tests matter more than the rest, because they attack the contract instead of exercising it:

  • test_reentrant_token_cannot_settle_a_lease_twice registers a hostile token whose transfer calls back into settle_lease while the first settlement is still paying out. The attack is attempted once, and the test asserts the re-entrant call errored and the lease ended up settled exactly once. This is the only executable proof of the checks-effects-interactions ordering, and it is the property that makes a malicious token non-exploitable rather than merely inconvenient.
  • the full lifecycle test escrowed with the real Stellar Asset Contract (env.register_stellar_asset_contract_v2) rather than contracts/mock_token, so the money paths are checked against a token this project does not control.

docs.title: What that coverage does not establish
docs.text:
A green suite is easy to over-read, so the limits are stated explicitly.

  • The threat model may be incomplete. The 14 rows are the threats the authors thought of. The main value of an audit is the rows it adds, and by definition none of those are here yet.
  • Arbitrary tokens are out of scope. set_token accepts any SEP-41 address. The suite proves the registry survives a re-entrant token; it cannot prove anything about a token that deviates from the interface in ways the registry does not expect.
  • Only simulated-ledger behaviour is tested. The tests run against the soroban-sdk Env, not a deployed network, so instruction-footprint limits, eviction under real storage pressure, and consensus-timing edges are not covered here. The soroban-sdk test host does not enforce maxEntryTtl on extend_ttl at all, so the TTL clamp is asserted from the policy value rather than demonstrated as a host rejection. Read the TTL rules in the contract reference as analysis, not as measurement.
  • State growth is bounded per call, not in aggregate. bump_service and bump_lease are permissionless and each one charges its rent to the caller, which is what makes them safe to expose — but nothing here bounds how many entries may be kept alive or by whom. Persistent state that outlives its usefulness is an operational cost, and the suite does not price it.
  • Client code and provider middleware are not this contract. Anything integrating per Integration is outside the audited surface, and outside the surface these guarantees describe.
  • The documentation itself is unaudited. A page that describes behaviour the code does not have is precisely the defect an audit catches and a test suite cannot.

docs.title: What a mainnet deployment would require
docs.text:
Deployments records Mainnet as ⛔ not deployed, and Deployment → Mainnet gives the reason: deployment is deferred until the contract is audited. Audited is a process, not a badge, so the gate list a mainnet launch would have to clear first is:

  1. An independent audit by a contract-security firm, with the report published and linked from the release notes and SECURITY.md. A private report that stays private does not count as clearing this.
  2. Findings fixed and re-proved. Every High and Medium with a code fix and a test in contracts/registry/src/test.rs that fails without the fix. Per the developer guide, each security-sensitive change gets an adversarial case, not just a happy path.
  3. Upgrade trust bounded. Today a single admin key can swap the Wasm and rewrite the escrow rules. Before mainnet value is in range, that key should be multisig or timelocked, and the timelock itself reviewed (see Known limitations).
  4. A live operation path. Someone watching the event stream, a named owner for the deployment, and a written response procedure. There is no protocol-wide pause: set_service_active(provider, service_id, false) blocks new leases on one service and leaves in-flight leases valid, and upgrade is admin-only. That is a throttle, not a kill switch.
  5. A staged value ramp. Deploy, cap total escrow to something you would accept losing, run real lease cycles against the cap, and only then raise it.
  6. A verifiable record. The mainnet contract id, Wasm hash and version in docs/deployments.md, each confirmed on-chain through version(), get_admin() and get_token() rather than taken from the page.

Until 1 through 4 are done, this contract is for Testnet and for limited-value evaluation. On Testnet every failure mode above costs an afternoon of redeploying fake XLM; on Mainnet it costs someone's deposit.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
These are real and tracked as Drips Wave issues rather than hidden.

  • Upgrade trust. The admin can replace the contract Wasm. While using a multisig admin prevents a single compromised key from executing an unauthorized upgrade, adding an on-chain timelock to upgrades remains future work.
  • No provider key rotation. A service is bound to the address that registered it. Transferring a service is a wave-medium issue.
  • No rate updates. Changing rate_per_call requires registering a new service; in-flight leases keep their original escrow.
  • Settlement is a single report. The contract trusts the provider's verified_calls; it cannot independently observe HTTP usage. Consumers are protected by the fixed allotment and the refund path, not by proof of non-delivery.
  • Not audited, and nothing on this page substitutes for it. See Audit status.

docs.title: Deployment hygiene
docs.text:
• Only trust contract ids in docs/deployments.md.
  • The admin key should be a cold or multisig Stellar account. It can change the escrow token and propose/cancel upgrades, but execution waits 24h on-ledger.
  • Verify the deployed metadata and configuration after deploy:
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account admin --network testnet -- version
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account admin --network testnet -- get_admin
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account admin --network testnet -- get_token
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account admin --network testnet -- get_service --service_id 1

Testnet resets (2–4 times a year, at 17:00 UTC) wipe all ledger entries and change the contract id. Redeploy after a reset. See Networks.

docs.title: Disclosure
docs.text: Report vulnerabilities privately per SECURITY.md. We will credit reporters in the release notes unless asked not to.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Every failure this contract can return, grouped by who is holding the error. Each entry names the fix and the command that proves the state you are about to act on. Error codes link to the contract reference table, which is the authoritative list.

Nothing here moves funds. settle_lease pays a provider and revoke_expired_lease refunds a consumer, and both can only be called once per lease — so verify first, then call.

docs.title: Three commands first
docs.text:
Most "the contract is broken" reports are a wrong contract id, a wrong network or an unconfigured token. These three answers cost one simulation each:

export REGISTRY=<contract id from docs/deployments.md>
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet -- version
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet -- get_admin
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet -- get_token
What you see What it means Go to version returns the release you deployed the id is live and initialised keep reading any call returns Error(WasmNotInstalled) or the ledger says the entry does not exist wrong id, or the network was reset The network moved under you get_admin returns NotInitialized this contract was never initialised NotInitialized and AlreadyInitialized get_token returns TokenNotSet leases can be read but never funded TokenNotSet

Read calls still need a funded --source-account, because the CLI builds a simulation transaction: see the note on read calls in Networks.

docs.title: LeaseNotExpired
docs.text:
Cause: revoke_expired_lease ran before expires_at. The lease is still inside its term, so the provider may still be paid.

Fix: wait for the term to end, or use the calls you paid for and let the provider settle.

Verify the term:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- get_lease --lease_id 1
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- lease_status --lease_id 1

Reference: error code 9.

docs.title: RevokeWindowNotElapsed
docs.text:
Cause: the lease is expired, but fewer than SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS (24 hours) have passed since expires_at. That window belongs to the provider: they can still settle for the calls they served.

Fix: wait until expires_at + 24h. The refund is the whole locked_deposit — revocation is all-or-nothing and pays the provider nothing, which is why the window exists.

Verify how much is still yours:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- locked_balance --lease_id 1

Reference: error code 10.

docs.title: Unauthorized on revoke_expired_lease
docs.text:
Cause: the lease belongs to a different address than the one that authorised. A lease is not transferable, and the refund path follows lease.consumer, not the caller.

Fix: re-run with the account that created the lease. If you lost that key, there is no recovery path on chain — that is a trust assumption, not a bug.

Verify who owns it: compare consumer in the get_lease output with stellar keys address <your-seed-name>.

Reference: error code 3.

docs.title: InvalidCalls, InvalidDuration, DurationTooLong on create_lease
docs.text:
Code Cause Fix InvalidCalls requested_calls is 0 ask for at least one call InvalidDuration duration_secs is 0 the lease must have a term DurationTooLong term exceeds MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS (30 days) renew instead of lengthening: the storage TTL is only guaranteed for the bounded term

create_lease escrows rate_per_call × requested_calls before anything else, so a rejected lease moves no funds. To check the price before you buy:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- get_service --service_id 1

docs.title: ServiceNotFound or ServiceInactive on create_lease
docs.text:
Cause: the id is from another deployment, or the provider paused the service. Testnet resets restart service_id from zero, so an id you saved last week can point at a different service — or at nothing.

Fix: re-read the ids for the network you are on:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- service_count

ServiceInactive is the provider's set_service_status(false). Nothing is stuck: your funds never left your account.

docs.title: Overflow on create_lease
docs.text:
Cause: rate_per_call × requested_calls does not fit in i128. All deposit math is checked and a failed multiplication returns this instead of a cheaper lease.

Fix: request fewer calls. If a provider's rate is large enough that a normal order overflows, that is a pricing bug on their side — quote it as rate_per_call × calls before you escrow.

docs.title: DepositTooLarge on create_lease
docs.text:
Cause: the deposit fits in i128 but exceeds MAX_LEASE_DEPOSIT (1,000,000,000,000 base units, so 100,000 XLM at seven decimals). Overflow means the multiplication does not fit; this means it fits and is still more than one lease is allowed to escrow.

Fix: split the order into several leases of fewer calls each. The bound is deliberate: it caps what a single lease can put at risk, so raising it is a contract change, not a client setting.

docs.title: Your balance did not move but the lease exists
docs.text:
Cause: the transaction was not sent. stellar contract invoke simulates by default and prints the result without submitting.

Fix: add --send=yes, then confirm the lease landed:

stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger>

A lease_created event is the record that the escrow happened; see Following the event stream.

docs.title: LeaseNotSettleable on settle_lease
docs.text:
Cause: neither settlement condition holds yet. A lease settles when it has expired, or when the consumer used every call it paid for (verified_calls == allocated_calls).

Fix: settle at expiry with the real number of served calls — an under-report refunds the consumer and is not recoverable later, because a lease settles once.

Verify what you may claim:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider \
  --network testnet -- get_lease --lease_id 1
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider \
  --network testnet -- remaining_calls --lease_id 1

remaining_calls returns 0 for an expired lease, so use used_calls for the quota, not for the payout.

Reference: error code 8.

docs.title: InvalidCalls on settle_lease
docs.text:
Cause: verified_calls exceeds allocated_calls. Settlement cannot pay out more than the consumer escrowed.

Fix: pass at most allocated_calls. If your counter is higher than the allotment, your local count and the lease disagree — the on-chain record wins.

docs.title: Unauthorized on settle_lease
docs.text:
Cause: the authorising account is not service.provider for that lease.

Fix: settle with the key that registered the service. Two things make this surprisingly common:

  • a service was registered by one key and the settlement daemon runs with another
  • keys cannot be rotated yet; a service is bound to its registering address forever (known limitation)

Verify the binding:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider \
  --network testnet -- get_service --service_id 1

docs.title: Your funds never arrived after settling
docs.text:
Cause: the settlement paid verified_calls × rate_per_call, and the rest went back to the consumer. A settle with verified_calls = 0 pays you nothing.

Fix: check the amounts against the event, not your logs:

stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger>

A lease_settled event carries payout and refund. If the event is absent, the transaction was simulated and never sent (--send=yes).

docs.title: 429 / 403 from your own service, not the chain
docs.text: The contract only escrows; the HTTP layer is yours. The verification pipeline fails closed at each step, so the causes are: lease expired or settled (403), the caller is not lease.consumer (403), or the allotment is exhausted (429). A lease id that is not in docs/deployments.md's network is 403 with a LeaseNotFound on chain.

docs.title: NotInitialized and AlreadyInitialized
docs.text: Code Cause Fix NotInitialized init never ran on this id, or you are pointed at an old one check version above, then run init or correct REGISTRY AlreadyInitialized init ran twice, usually a re-run of the deploy script against an id that already exists stop; deploy a fresh contract instead. The admin cannot be changed by re-initialising

docs.title: TokenNotSet
docs.text:
Cause: the escrow asset was never configured. create_lease refuses to store a lease it cannot fund.

Fix: set the token, then verify it resolved to the address you meant:

stellar contract id asset --network testnet --asset native
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- set_token --admin $ADMIN --token <TOKEN_ID>
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet -- get_token

Changing the token while leases are in flight strands their payouts against the old asset. Settle or revoke first: see set_token.

docs.title: Unauthorized on set_token or upgrade
docs.text:
Cause: the caller is not the stored Admin.

Fix: stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account <whoever> --network testnet -- get_admin prints the only address that can authorise. If that key is lost, the token and the Wasm are frozen — escrow can still be refunded by consumers through revoke_expired_lease.

docs.title: upgrade succeeded but behaviour did not change
docs.text:
Cause: the hash you uploaded is not the build you think it is, or the version() string was not bumped before building.

Fix: compare what is on chain with what you built:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet -- version

version is embedded from Cargo.toml by contractmeta!, so it proves which release is live. Upgrades must keep the storage layout and must never renumber error codes (upgrading).

docs.title: The network moved under you
docs.text:
Testnet and Futurenet are reset by SDF 2–4 times a year, at 17:00 UTC. A reset deletes every ledger entry: the contract, its services, its leases and the account that funded them. The contract id changes, so the symptom is not one error but all of them at once — LeaseNotFound for ids that worked yesterday, ServiceNotFound for ids in Deployments, and clients that look like they are reading a broken protocol.

# Is this network a fresh one? Its ledger is near zero after a reset.
curl -s -X POST "$KEYLEASE_RPC_URL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"getLatestLedger","params":{}}'

# Is this the network you think it is?
curl -s -X POST "$KEYLEASE_RPC_URL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"getNetwork","params":{}}'

The passphrase in the getNetwork reply must match the row for your network in Networks. After a reset: redeploy with scripts/deploy-testnet.sh, re-issue set_token and register_service, fund accounts again, then update KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID and Deployments.

docs.title: Reads work, then start failing with 429
docs.text:
Cause: the public Testnet and Futurenet RPC endpoints are rate-limited and are not meant for a busy provider (production notes).

Fix: move to an authenticated provider and point KEYLEASE_RPC_URL at it. Back off on 429 rather than retrying immediately, and cache get_lease for a few seconds instead of re-reading per request.

docs.title: Your service rejects requests while RPC is down
docs.text: That is correct. The contract is not reachable during an RPC outage, so a provider cannot verify a lease and must not serve it (verification pipeline, step 2). No funds move: settlement and revocation still work as soon as any RPC responds, and a consumer's refund path never depends on a provider's infrastructure.

docs.title: Events are missing after a restart
docs.text:
Cause: the start ledger predates the contract's creation, or is ahead of the events you need.

Fix: re-read from the deploy ledger and check the count:

stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger>

Event names, topics and payloads are part of the ABI and only ever gain fields; decode by position-tolerant lookup, and treat a settled lease as final (Integration).

docs.title: Storage reads return nothing
docs.text:
Cause: raw getContractData needs the exact wire key. #[contracttype] enums encode as a vector whose first element is the variant symbol, so DataKey::Lease(7) is Vec[Symbol("Lease"), u64(7)].

Fix: prefer the read views (get_lease, get_service, lease_status) over raw storage. If you must read the key directly, the mapping table is in Reading contract state and events.

docs.title: Error code index
docs.text: The full table, with the precondition each code guards, is in the contract reference. Codes are part of the ABI: they are appended and never reused, so a number you see today is the same number after an upgrade.

docs.title: Design note — Revenue splits across multiple providers (#133)
docs.text:
Status: Proposed — awaiting maintainer approval. No contract code is changed by this note. Per CONTRIBUTING, a maintainer must approve this design before implementation begins.

Issue: #133 — Allow revenue splits across multiple providers Target release: v0.3.0 · Touches: lib.rs, types.rs, storage.rs, events.rs, errors.rs

docs.title: 1. Problem statement
docs.text:
A service has exactly one provider address, and settle_lease pays that address the whole payout. Teams that share operational and infrastructure costs — an API owner plus an RPC operator, a marketplace front end plus an upstream data source — have to route money off-chain after settlement, which is manual, opaque to indexers and outside the protocol's accounting.

This note proposes a bounded revenue split stored per service: an ordered list of recipients with basis-point shares that always sums to 10 000. A service with no split configured keeps the current single-provider behaviour exactly.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Pay multiple recipients atomically in the settlement transaction.
  • Keep the existing single-provider layout and settlement flow as the default, with no migration and no change to Service or Lease.
  • Bound the work per settlement: fixed maximum recipients, no unbounded loop.
  • Make the split and every per-recipient payout observable off-chain.
  • Guarantee the distributed total never exceeds the settlement payout and that rounding never strands or creates value.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Changing who may settle a lease (service.provider remains the only settler).
  • Transferring service ownership or splitting governance rights; recipients get revenue only.
  • Per-lease split snapshots or recipient-level escrow accounts.
  • Splitting the consumer refund (it always goes to the consumer).

docs.title: 2.1 Representation
docs.text:
/// One entry in a service's revenue split.
#[contracttype]
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
pub struct RevenueShare {
    pub recipient: Address,
    /// Share of every payout, in basis points. All shares sum to 10_000.
    pub share_bps: u32,
}
  • Basis points: 1 bps = 0.01 %, and 10_000 bps = 100 %.
  • Recipient count: 1..=MAX_SPLIT_RECIPIENTS, with MAX_SPLIT_RECIPIENTS = 10 (see §6 for why 10).
  • Sum: sum(share_bps) == 10_000 exactly, computed with checked_add.
  • Non-zero: every share_bps > 0; a zero-share recipient is rejected rather than silently paid nothing.
  • Duplicates: the same recipient address may appear once. A duplicate is rejected at configuration time, which also prevents duplicate payments at settlement.
  • Self-payment: a recipient equal to the registry's own address is rejected, because a transfer to self would be a no-op that breaks the distributed == payout accounting story.

The split is stored outside Service:

Key Storage Value TTL RevenueSplit(u64) persistent Vec<RevenueShare> extended on write and read, 30-day horizon, matching Service

Service keeps exactly its current five fields. That is what makes the change upgrade-safe: existing Service entries decode unchanged, and the split key is simply absent for every service that never configures one.

docs.title: 2.2 Backward compatibility: the single-provider default
docs.text:
An absent RevenueSplit(service_id) key is the legacy configuration:

no split stored  =>  pay 100 % to service.provider, as today

Consequences:

  • register_service is unchanged; a provider does not have to configure anything.
  • Existing services continue to settle with one transfer and the exact same lease_settled event payload.
  • Existing leases are unaffected; the split is read at settlement time, and a service without a split behaves identically to v0.2.x.
  • A provider that wants the old behaviour back can call set_revenue_split with a single entry { provider, 10_000 }, or clear_revenue_split to remove the key entirely. Both produce the same payout; the event differs.

docs.title: 2.3 Settlement
docs.text:
settle_lease keeps all of its current checks, ordering and refund logic. Only the payout step changes:

payout = service.rate_per_call * verified_calls      // unchanged, checked
refund = lease.locked_deposit - payout               // unchanged, checked

persist lease.used_calls, lease.settled = true       // unchanged, before transfers

if a split is stored for lease.service_id:
    distributed = 0
    for i in 0 .. shares.len():
        amount[i] = (payout * shares[i].share_bps) / 10_000    // floor, checked
        distributed += amount[i]                               // checked
    amount[last] += payout - distributed                       // remainder
    for each non-zero amount[i]:
        transfer(contract -> shares[i].recipient, amount[i])
else:
    transfer(contract -> service.provider, payout)             // unchanged

Rounding rule. The first n-1 recipients receive floor(payout * share_bps / 10_000); the last recipient in the configured list receives its own floor plus the entire remainder payout - sum(floors). Because the shares sum to 10 000,

sum(floor(payout * bps_i / 10_000))  <=  payout  <  sum(floors) + n

so the remainder is in 0..n, and the last payment remains at most payout plus a few stroops of rounding. Total distributed is exactly payout; nothing is stranded in the contract and nothing is minted. The rule is deterministic and depends only on the stored order, so any indexer can reproduce every amount from lease_settled plus the stored split. If payout == 0, no transfers occur.

Ordering and atomicity. The split is read before the first transfer and is not re-read afterwards, so a re-entrant token cannot change recipients mid-settlement. settled = true is still persisted before any transfer, so a re-entrant settle_lease reverts. If any transfer fails, the whole Soroban invocation reverts: no recipient is paid, the lease stays unsettled, and the refund does not happen either.

Refund. The consumer refund is unchanged and is paid once, after the payout distribution. It is never split.

docs.title: 2.4 Changing the split
docs.text:
set_revenue_split is callable only by the current service.provider. It replaces the entire list atomically; there is no per-entry editing, so a partial write can never leave the shares summing to something other than 10 000.

The split applies to settlements that happen after the change. In-flight leases are paid under the split in force at settlement time. This is deliberate: the escrow is owed to the provider, and routing that revenue among the provider's own recipients is the provider's commercial decision. The consumer's refund and the total payout are unaffected, so no consumer is harmed by a mid-lease change. The trade-off against snapshotting per lease is discussed in §8.

docs.title: 3. Storage changes
docs.text:
Key Storage Value Notes RevenueSplit(u64) persistent Vec<RevenueShare> new, additive; TTL extended on save and read

No existing key changes, no field is added to Service or Lease, and the DataKey discriminants keep their wire names. A v0.3.0 Wasm can be installed over a deployment that holds live services and leases; services without the new key settle exactly as before.

The stored vector is bounded by MAX_SPLIT_RECIPIENTS, so a split entry has a fixed maximum encoded size (about ten address+bps pairs) and a predictable rent cost.

docs.title: Entry points
docs.text:
Entry point Auth Description set_revenue_split(provider, service_id, shares: Vec<RevenueShare>) provider (must own the service) Validate and store a complete split. Emits revenue_split_updated. clear_revenue_split(provider, service_id) provider (must own the service) Remove the split and fall back to 100 % to service.provider. Emits revenue_split_cleared. get_revenue_split(service_id) — Option<Vec<RevenueShare>>; None means the single-provider default.

Read-only helper (optional, recommended for indexers):

View Returns payees(service_id) Vec<Address> — the configured recipients, or [service.provider] when no split is stored

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Event Topics Data revenue_split_updated service_id provider, shares: Vec<RevenueShare>, recipient_count, total_bps revenue_split_cleared service_id provider lease_split_paid lease_id total_payout, recipients: Vec<Address>, amounts: Vec<i128>
  • revenue_split_updated carries the full configured list, so an indexer can reconstruct every future payment from one event without extra RPC reads. total_bps is included (always 10 000) as a self-check for consumers.
  • lease_split_paid is emitted only when a split is configured and carries the exact per-recipient amounts actually transferred (including the remainder assignment). Indexers therefore never have to re-implement the rounding rule to reconcile balances. It is emitted alongside the unchanged lease_settled; the two share the lease_id topic, and lease_settled.payout equals lease_split_paid.total_payout.
  • For the legacy single-provider path neither new settlement event is emitted, so the existing event stream is unchanged.
  • Neither event carries secret material: recipients and shares are already public on-chain configuration.

docs.title: Error codes (appended, never renumbered)
docs.text:
Code Variant Meaning 33 EmptySplit Zero recipients supplied 34 TooManyRecipients More than MAX_SPLIT_RECIPIENTS 35 InvalidShares A share is zero, or the total is not exactly 10 000 36 DuplicateRecipient The same address appears twice 37 InvalidRecipient A recipient is the registry itself

(17–32 are reserved by the #137 proposal; the final numbers are assigned when both designs are approved so the two changes never collide.)

docs.title: 5. Authorization and governance model
docs.text:
Actor Can do Cannot do service.provider Set/clear the split for its service Change another service's split Recipient Receive its share at settlement Change the split, settle, or claim outside settlement Admin set_token, upgrade Change a split or move payouts Consumer Create/revoke leases Change the split or redirect the refund

No new governance role is introduced. Setting a split is an ordinary provider-signed transaction, exactly like set_service_active, and the service owner remains the only account that can settle, so the payer and the person choosing the payees are the same actor.

docs.title: 6. Security considerations
docs.text:
Unauthorized changes. set_revenue_split / clear_revenue_split call require_auth() on provider and then check service.provider == provider. A third party cannot redirect a service's revenue, and the admin cannot either.

Invalid or excessive allocations. Validation happens before any write: non-empty, <= 10 entries, every share_bps > 0, checked_add sum exactly 10_000, no duplicates, no self-recipient. A rejected call leaves the stored split untouched. The store-then-overwrite design is atomic per call, so there is never an intermediate sum other than the old or the new valid list.

Duplicate payments. Rejected at configuration time, and the settlement loop walks each vector index exactly once. Because the payout is computed and validated before the loop, no recipient can be paid more than its stored share (plus the single remainder allocation to the last entry).

No value creation or loss. sum(amounts) == payout, enforced by the remainder assignment and checked arithmetic; payout + refund == locked_deposit still holds. payout and every amount[i] use checked_mul/checked_add; an overflow reverts the transaction rather than truncating a recipient's payment.

Reentrancy and atomicity. settled = true is persisted before any transfer, and the split vector is read once, before the transfers, so a hostile recipient or token contract cannot alter the list or settle twice. All payments and the refund happen in one transaction; a failure reverts the entire distribution and the refund. The adversarial re-entrant-token test is extended to a split with two recipients.

Resource limits. MAX_SPLIT_RECIPIENTS = 10 bounds the settlement to at most ten payout transfers plus one refund. That is the main cost driver: each SEP-41 transfer is a cross-contract call, and Soroban charges instructions and ledger entries per call. Ten keeps a split settlement comfortably within a standard transaction while covering realistic team structures. The trade-off against a larger bound is in §8; the implementation must include a test that settles a 10-recipient split so the budget is measured, not assumed.

Griefing and storage. The list is provider-owned and bounded, so no one can inflate a service's storage through the split. RevenueSplit is persistent with the same 30-day TTL policy as Service; it cannot be evicted while the service is being read or settled, and a split costs its provider a bounded rent.

Rounding edge cases. payout < number of recipients produces zeros for some entries; zero-amount transfers are skipped and the last entry receives the few stroops of remainder. A single-recipient split at 10 000 bps is mathematically identical to the legacy path; a one-recipient split at any other value is rejected by the sum check. payout == 0 emits no split payments but still emits lease_settled and the refund.

Interaction with #137. A stake is attached to service.provider, not to split recipients. Slashing debits the provider's stake, never a recipient's payout, and the revenue split does not affect stake availability or dispute resolution. Only the provider can settle and therefore only the provider can trigger a distribution.

docs.title: 7. Testing strategy
docs.text:
New tests in contracts/registry/src/test.rs, keeping the existing suite green:

Configuration

  • a service with no split settles exactly as before: one transfer to the provider, unchanged lease_settled payload, no lease_split_paid;
  • set_revenue_split with one entry {provider, 10_000} behaves like the default and emits revenue_split_updated;
  • two and three recipients with valid shares are stored and readable through get_revenue_split / payees;
  • the full event payload (topics + shares + count + total) is asserted with assert_single_event;
  • invalid totals (9 999, 10 001), a zero share, an empty list, eleven recipients, a duplicate address and a self-recipient each revert with the documented error and leave the previous split intact;
  • a non-owner, an impostor and the admin all fail to set or clear a split (Unauthorized);
  • clear_revenue_split restores the legacy behaviour and emits the event.

Settlement

  • a two-recipient split (e.g. 7 000 / 3 000) pays each the right amount and the consumer gets the correct refund; escrow == 0 afterwards;
  • three recipients with a payout that does not divide evenly (e.g. payout 100, shares 3 333 / 3 333 / 3 334) pays 33 / 33 / 34 and emits matching lease_split_paid.amounts;
  • a rounding case where every floor truncates (payout 1, two recipients) gives the remainder to the last recipient, and the total still equals the payout;
  • verified_calls == 0 (full refund) performs no payout transfers and emits no lease_split_paid;
  • a 10-recipient split settles successfully (resource-limit test) with the total exactly equal to payout;
  • the real-SAC lifecycle test is repeated with a split token, proving the distribution works against the SAC;
  • the re-entrant token cannot settle twice when a split is configured and the first recipient is hostile;
  • a recipient that is a contract is paid exactly once.

Invariants asserted after every settlement test

  • sum(recipient payments) + refund == locked_deposit;
  • lease.locked_deposit, lease.settled and the provider's stake (when #137 is present) are unchanged by the split;
  • the registry's token balance returns to zero.

docs.title: 8. Open questions and trade-offs
docs.text:
1. Recipient bound. 10 covers most teams and bounds settlement to 11 cross-contract calls. A larger bound (e.g. 20) is more flexible but raises the fee of every settlement and the chance of exceeding the transaction budget. Question for maintainers: is 10 right, or should it be 5?
  2. Snapshot vs live split. Reading the split at settlement lets a provider re-route revenue mid-lease; snapshotting it into the lease would require a new Lease field (breaking the stored encoding) or a new per-lease key and more storage. This note chooses live configuration because only the payer's own routing changes and the consumer's refund is untouched. Alternative: LeaseSplit(lease_id) written at create_lease for full per-lease determinism.
  3. Remainder policy. Paying the remainder to the last configured entry is the simplest deterministic rule and easy to reproduce. Alternatives: the largest share, or largest-remainder (Hamilton) apportionment, which is marginally fairer but more code and more subtle to test.
  4. Dust when all shares floor to zero. With payout < n, early recipients can receive 0 while the last receives the whole payout. That is exact and harmless, but a provider may be surprised. Alternative: reject settlements whose payout is smaller than the recipient count — rejected here because it would couple settlement to the split and could block a refund.
  5. Recipients as contracts. Paying a contract recipient is allowed; whether it should require the recipient to implement a specific interface (or be rejected) is a policy question. This note allows any Address, consistent with the rest of the protocol.
  6. Per-recipient events. One lease_split_paid carrying parallel arrays is compact and cheap; n separate events would be easier for naive indexers but costs n event emissions per settlement. This note prefers the single event; the schema should be documented before release.
  7. Split plus future service transfer. If service transfer ships (#issue for key rotation), the new owner inherits the split. The design should state that explicitly, and whether a transfer must clear or re-confirm the split.
  8. Versioning. The change is additive, but the workspace version should move to 0.3.0 with the #137 work and the release notes must describe the split semantics and rounding rule.

docs.title: 9. Review request
docs.text:
Per CONTRIBUTING.md, this note needs maintainer approval before code:

  • Confirm MAX_SPLIT_RECIPIENTS (10 vs 5) and the one-event-with-arrays shape.
  • Confirm that the split is read at settlement time rather than snapshotted per lease.
  • Confirm the rounding rule (remainder to the last configured recipient).
  • Confirm the error-code range so it does not collide with #137.

Once approved, implementation lands on the same feature branch as #137, with the tests above and the full four-command validation from CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Design note — Provider staking and slashing (#137)
docs.text:
Status: Proposed — awaiting maintainer approval. No contract code is changed by this note. Per CONTRIBUTING, a maintainer must approve this design before implementation begins.

Issue: #137 — Add provider staking and slashing for proven over-reporting Target release: v0.3.0 · Touches: lib.rs, storage.rs, types.rs, events.rs, errors.rs

docs.title: 1. Problem statement
docs.text:
settle_lease trusts the provider's verified_calls. The allotment caps the damage per lease, and the consumer can reclaim an unsettled deposit after the grace window, but a provider that reports more calls than it actually served keeps the over-payment. The only penalty is that the consumer does not come back. There is no on-chain cost to over-reporting within allocated_calls, so the protocol's central trust assumption — "the provider reports honestly" — has no economic backstop.

This note proposes an opt-in provider stake that a service must post before it accepts leases, plus a bounded, evidence-based slashing process for proven over-reporting.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Give consumers a recourse that is funded by the provider, not by other users.
  • Make the penalty proportional to the over-report and hard-capped, so the mechanism cannot be used to confiscate a provider's business.
  • Keep staking opt-in: existing services and deployments keep working unchanged, and unstaked services continue to be leaseable.
  • Never delay, block or alter settlement or the consumer refund path.
  • Add no unbounded loops, no new trust in off-chain data, and no change to the existing Service/Lease storage layout.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Proving real HTTP usage on-chain. The contract cannot observe traffic; the design constrains who may accuse, how much may be slashed and where the money goes, and relies on a public evidence hash plus an arbiter.
  • Insuring consumers for non-delivery. That remains the refund path plus, now, a stake.
  • A general arbitration court, appeals beyond one challenge round, or slashing for anything other than over-reporting.

docs.title: 2.1 Stake custody
docs.text:
Stake is held by the registry in the same SEP-41 token as escrow, but accounted for separately. Escrow accounting is per lease (locked_deposit); stake accounting is per provider. The contract must never infer one from the token balance — sum(locked deposits) + sum(stakes) == token balance is an invariant the tests assert; the token balance itself is never used as a source of truth.

Stake is associated with the provider address (Service.provider), not the service id. One pool covers every service that provider opts in, which avoids duplicating capital across services and keeps the slash/withdraw bookkeeping bounded. Revenue-split recipients (#133) are payees only; they are not stakers and cannot be slashed.

docs.title: 2.2 Opt-in per service
docs.text:
A provider opts a service into staking with opt_in_service_stake. The opt-in is a separate storage key (ServiceStake(service_id)) rather than a new field on Service, so existing Service entries keep decoding and the storage layout is upgrade-safe. Opting out only blocks new leases.

create_lease enforces the invariant for opted-in services:

if service is staked:
    provider stake must exist and available_stake >= min_stake
    the provider must not have a withdrawal pending

If either check fails the lease reverts (InsufficientStake / StakeWithdrawalPending). Existing services that never opt in are unaffected; no new lease on an unstaked service ever requires stake.

docs.title: 2.3 Minimum and configurable requirements
docs.text:
The admin configures a single StakeConfig in instance storage:

Field Meaning Default Bound min_stake Minimum available stake an opted-in service needs at lease creation — > 0 dispute_bond Bond an accuser posts to open a dispute — > 0 dispute_window_secs How long after a lease's dispute anchor a dispute may be opened — 1 h – 30 days challenge_period_secs Provider response window before resolution — 1 h – 7 days unbonding_period_secs Delay between withdrawal request and release — >= dispute_window + challenge_period, max 30 days max_slash_bps Hard cap on the share of a provider's stake one dispute may slash — 1 – 10 000 bps

Staking is disabled until the admin sets a config; opt_in_service_stake and open_dispute revert with StakeNotConfigured before then. This means an upgraded deployment behaves exactly like today until the operator opts the protocol in. The admin can raise/lower min_stake later; lowering it takes effect immediately for new leases, raising it never invalidates existing leases.

docs.title: 2.4 Evidence and slashing authority
docs.text:
The contract cannot validate usage data, so "proven" is defined procedurally. A dispute may only be opened by the lease's consumer — the party that paid and therefore has standing — and only against a settled lease of a staked service, within the dispute window.

Admissible evidence. The contract stores only a 32-byte commitment (evidence_hash) and emits it. The evidence bundle is published off-chain in a documented format so any third party can reproduce the verdict:

  • the lease id, service id and settlement transaction hash,
  • the provider's reported verified_calls,
  • per-call records the provider signed or that the consumer can verify (signed request logs, provider receipts, or the provider's own metering export),
  • a manifest hash over those artifacts, which is the evidence_hash.

The provider may answer once with contest_dispute, supplying its own counter_evidence_hash. Both hashes and the final verdict are permanent event data.

Who may slash.

  1. The consumer opens the dispute and posts dispute_bond.
  2. The provider may contest during challenge_period_secs.
  3. The arbiter — a dedicated role, defaulting to the admin and rotatable by the admin — resolves after the challenge period with resolve_dispute.
  4. Only then, and only if approved, is stake moved.

Bounds that prevent arbitrary confiscation.

  • Only a consumer with a settled lease can accuse; the arbiter cannot open a dispute against a provider it dislikes.
  • The disputed amount is bounded by the on-chain over-report: overreported_calls * rate_per_call, where overreported_calls <= lease.allocated_calls.
  • The slash is additionally capped at stake_total * max_slash_bps / 10_000 and can never exceed the provider's remaining stake.
  • Slashed value is paid to the accusing consumer, never to the admin, the arbiter or the registry. The arbiter therefore cannot profit from a ruling.
  • A rejected dispute returns nothing to the accuser: the bond is paid to the provider as compensation for the false accusation, and the provider's stake is untouched.
  • Every step emits an event with the evidence hashes and amounts; the arbiter role and config are admin-visible and rotatable.

A single challenge round is deliberately the whole procedure. It is a bounded governance process, not a court: the cap, the consumer-only standing and the "proceeds to the accuser" rule are what make it safe to keep small.

docs.title: 2.5 Withdrawal rules
docs.text:
Stake leaves in two steps:

  1. request_stake_withdrawal(provider, amount) requires:
  2. the provider has opted out of every service (staked_services == 0),
  3. no unsettled leases are attributable to the provider (open_leases == 0),
  4. no dispute against the provider is pending (pending_disputes == 0),
  5. amount <= available, and amount > 0. It moves amount from available to unbonding and sets unbonding_until = now + unbonding_period_secs. A withdrawal request also makes create_lease revert with StakeWithdrawalPending for that provider's services, so no new exposure can be created while capital is leaving.
  6. withdraw_stake(provider) requires now >= unbonding_until, open_leases == 0 and pending_disputes == 0, then transfers the unbonding amount to the provider.

Because unbonding_period_secs >= dispute_window_secs + challenge_period_secs, every settlement that could still be disputed has either been disputed or is past its window before the capital is released, and unbonding stake remains slashable until the transfer happens. A new deposit_stake during unbonding cancels the request (unbonding returns to available, the timer clears), which is safe because the funds never left the contract.

pending_disputes and open_leases are per-provider counters, incremented and decremented on the paths that create and close them, so withdrawal never scans a collection.

docs.title: 2.6 Settlement and service lifecycle
docs.text:
• Settlement and revocation are unchanged: stake never gates settle_lease or revoke_expired_lease, and the consumer's exit remains guaranteed. A provider that has been slashed can still settle leases it already sold.
  • Slashing is paid from the provider's stake, not from lease escrow, so payout + refund == locked_deposit still holds for every lease.
  • If a slash drops available below min_stake, the service is effectively deactivated without writing to Service: the next create_lease reverts InsufficientStake. This avoids iterating a provider's services to flip is_active, keeps Service layout-compatible, and makes topping the stake up an immediate recovery. set_service_active(false) remains available for an explicit pause, and a provider can always opt out.
  • A provider's opt-in/opt-out never changes the terms of an existing lease; those leases settle under the rules in force when they were created.

docs.title: 3. Storage changes
docs.text:
All additions are new DataKey variants. Service, Lease, LeaseStatus and every existing key keep their exact wire encoding.

Key Storage Value TTL policy StakeConfig instance StakeConfig instance TTL, bumped on every state change Arbiter instance Address instance TTL Stake(Address) persistent StakeAccount extended on read/write, 30-day horizon ServiceStake(u64) persistent bool extended with the service, 30-day horizon DisputeCount instance u64 instance TTL Dispute(u64) persistent Dispute extended on read/write; retained through resolution + 30 days 
pub struct StakeAccount {
    pub available: i128,
    pub unbonding: i128,
    pub unbonding_until: u64,
    pub open_leases: u32,      // leases of this provider not yet settled/revoked
    pub staked_services: u32,  // services currently opted in
    pub pending_disputes: u32, // disputes not yet resolved
}

pub struct Dispute {
    pub dispute_id: u64,
    pub lease_id: u64,
    pub service_id: u64,
    pub accuser: Address,       // lease.consumer
    pub provider: Address,      // service.provider
    pub evidence_hash: BytesN<32>,
    pub counter_evidence_hash: BytesN<32>, // zeroed until contested
    pub overreported_calls: u32,
    pub slash_amount: i128,     // computed and frozen at open time
    pub bond: i128,
    pub opened_at: u64,
    pub status: DisputeStatus,  // Open = 0, Contested = 1, Approved = 2, Rejected = 3
}

pub struct StakeConfig {
    pub min_stake: i128,
    pub dispute_bond: i128,
    pub dispute_window_secs: u64,
    pub challenge_period_secs: u64,
    pub unbonding_period_secs: u64,
    pub max_slash_bps: u32,
}

slash_amount is frozen at open_dispute so topping up the stake, or a second dispute, cannot change what the first one may take. The bounded cap is re-evaluated against the balance at resolution and the payout is the smaller of the frozen amount and the remaining stake.

docs.title: 5. Authorization and governance model
docs.text:
Role Can do Cannot do Provider Deposit, opt in/out, request/cancel/complete withdrawal, contest a dispute, settle its leases Slash, resolve disputes, withdraw while exposed Consumer Open a dispute on its settled lease after posting the bond Open disputes on others' leases, slash directly Arbiter Resolve a dispute after the challenge period Open disputes, change config, touch escrow, keep slashed value Admin Set config, rotate the arbiter, upgrade the Wasm Slash, resolve disputes, move stake or escrow

The admin and arbiter should be separate keys (both cold/multisig) in production; the default of "arbiter = admin" exists so a fresh deployment works without a second key, and the role is rotatable and announced by arbiter_set. Governance is deliberately narrow: the only discretionary decision in the protocol is the one-bit approve in resolve_dispute, and its consequences are capped, recipient-fixed and permanently logged.

docs.title: 6. Backward compatibility
docs.text:
• Storage: only new keys. Service and Lease are untouched, so a v0.3.0 Wasm can be installed over a v0.2.x deployment with live services and leases.
  • Existing services: remain unstaked and continue to accept leases with no stake requirement. Nothing becomes mandatory.
  • Existing leases: unchanged terms; settlement, refund and revocation do not consult stake.
  • ABI: all new entry points, events and error codes are additive. No error number is reused and no event payload changes.
  • Default state: staking is inert until set_stake_config is called, so an upgraded deployment behaves identically to v0.2.x.
  • Events: the existing event stream for lease lifecycle is byte-identical; stake and dispute events are new names.

docs.title: 7. Security considerations
docs.text:
Re-entrancy and ordering. Every money path follows checks-effects-interactions. open_dispute persists the dispute and the bond before transferFrom-style movement (the consumer transfer happens after the counter and bond are recorded). resolve_dispute sets the dispute to Approved/Rejected, decrements pending_disputes and debits stake before any token transfer, so a malicious recipient contract cannot re-enter for a second slash or a second bond refund. withdraw_stake zeroes the unbonding balance before the transfer. A re-entrant token would see terminal state and revert the whole transaction.

Storage integrity. open_leases and pending_disputes are counters, not collections, and are maintained on both sides of each transition (create/settle/revoke, open/resolve). The tests assert they return to zero after a full lifecycle. Dispute records are immutable after resolution except for status. All persistent additions carry explicit TTL extensions; a stake entry is read/written on every path that needs it, and a dispute entry is extended when opened, contested and resolved.

Economic attack vectors.

Attack Mitigation Provider over-reports and withdraws before a dispute Unbonding ≥ dispute window + challenge period; unbonding remains slashable; withdrawal requires zero open leases and zero pending disputes; new leases are blocked while unbonding Consumer grieves a provider with disputes Bond forfeited to the provider on rejection; bounded cap; one contest round; evidence hash makes frivolous claims auditable Arbiter colludes with a consumer Slash proceeds go to the consumer, not the arbiter; per-dispute cap; admin-rotatable role; every ruling is event-logged with evidence hashes Provider keeps too little stake relative to revenue min_stake is admin-set and enforced on every new lease of a staked service; raising it never invalidates existing leases Slash is used to seize a business Only settled leases, consumer standing, over-report bound, max_slash_bps cap, one round, provider keeps all un-slashed stake and future revenue Double slash on one lease At most one dispute per lease (open_dispute rejects a lease that already has one, checked through a per-lease dispute index), and a terminal status Stake/escrow accounting confusion Separate internal ledgers; the token balance is never read as a source of truth; tests assert escrow + stake == balance Griefing by never contesting Resolution is permissionless in time but arbiter-driven; an uncontested dispute resolves on schedule

Governance and upgrade implications. StakeConfig, Arbiter and the new keys must keep their meaning across upgrades; the implementation must never renumber errors or change the Service/Lease encoding. A malicious upgrade can already change any rule, so the arbiter/admin keys deserve the same cold-storage treatment as the existing admin key. Because min_stake and max_slash_bps are live parameters, changes to them should be announced and are visible in stake_config_set.

Resource limits. Every new path is O(1) in storage reads/writes and does a constant number of token calls (at most two transfers in a resolution). No entry point iterates a user-controlled collection; recipient and service lists are never walked to enforce stake.

docs.title: 8. Testing strategy
docs.text:
New tests in contracts/registry/src/test.rs (plus the existing suite kept green):

Stake lifecycle

  • deposit credits available, moves tokens, emits stake_deposited, extends TTL;
  • deposit with zero/negative amount reverts InvalidStakeAmount;
  • opt-in requires a config and an account; opt-in/opt-out emit service_stake_changed;
  • create_lease on a staked service reverts InsufficientStake below min_stake and succeeds at exactly min_stake;
  • unstaked services keep leasing with no stake at all (backward compatibility).

Withdrawal

  • request moves available to unbonding, blocks new leases (StakeWithdrawalPending);
  • early withdraw_stake reverts WithdrawalNotReady;
  • withdraw succeeds after the delay and only then moves tokens;
  • request reverts while a lease is unsettled (OutstandingLeases), while a service is still opted in, and while a dispute is pending (PendingDispute);
  • deposit during unbonding cancels the request and restores available.

Disputes and slashing

  • only the lease consumer can open (InvalidDispute / Unauthorized);
  • a dispute on an unstaked service reverts ServiceNotStaked;
  • a dispute on an unsettled or out-of-window lease reverts DisputeWindowClosed;
  • the bond is transferred in and the frozen slash_amount respects both the over-report bound and max_slash_bps;
  • contest is provider-only and single-shot; resolution before the challenge period reverts ChallengePeriodActive;
  • approval pays the accuser the slash plus the returned bond, debits stake (available first, then unbonding), emits dispute_resolved and provider_slashed;
  • rejection pays the bond to the provider, leaves stake untouched, and clears the pending counter;
  • double resolution reverts DisputeClosed; a second dispute on the same lease reverts;
  • a re-entrant token cannot double-slash or double-refund a bond.

Settlement and lifecycle after a slash

  • an existing lease still settles and refunds correctly after its provider is slashed;
  • create_lease reverts InsufficientStake after the stake falls below min_stake (effective deactivation), and works again after a top-up;
  • opt_out_service_stake blocks new leases but leaves existing leases settleable;
  • payout + refund == locked_deposit and escrow + stake == token balance hold across the whole flow;
  • the real-SAC lifecycle test and the existing re-entrancy test still pass.

docs.title: 9. Open questions and trade-offs
docs.text:
1. Provider-level vs per-service stake. A single pool is capital-efficient and keeps checks O(1); a per-service pool isolates a bad service from a provider's other business. This note chooses provider-level and lets the provider opt out individual services. Rejected alternative: a stake field on Service (breaks stored-value layout) and a per-service pool (fragments capital and needs per-service withdrawal bookkeeping).
  2. Arbiter discretion. One challenge round with a capped, accuser-directed payout is cheap and bounded, but a corrupt arbiter can still approve a malicious dispute up to the cap. Alternatives: two-of-two (arbiter + admin) approval, a bonded arbiter, or a consumer/provider optimistic game with a fraud proof. Each adds interface and governance surface; we should decide before implementation whether disputes above a threshold need two approvals.
  3. Exposure-based stake. The design requires available >= min_stake, not "stake proportional to open escrow". Per-lease stake would price risk better but needs mid-lease top-ups and makes settlement conditional on stake. Question for maintainers: should a later version require min_stake >= k * open_leases?
  4. Dispute window anchor. Disputes are anchored at expires_at + grace + dispute_window, because Lease has no settled_at field and adding one would change its encoding. This grants a generous window to fully-consumed leases settled early. Alternative: add SettlementTime(lease_id) as a new key and anchor on the real settlement time.
  5. Bond size. A flat dispute_bond is simple but may be too small for large services or too large for small ones. Alternative: a bps-of-disputed-value bond with a floor and a ceiling.
  6. Who audits evidence. The on-chain record is a hash plus a verdict. If maintainers want verifiable evidence handling, the off-chain bundle format needs a documented schema and a canonical hashing rule before release.
  7. Unbonding UX. Requiring open_leases == 0 and full opt-out before a withdrawal request is conservative and can lock capital for up to a lease term plus the delay. Alternative: allow withdrawal requests with open leases by reserving the newest leases' exposure.
  8. Versioning. This is a breaking-in-behaviour (not ABI) change once a config is set; the workspace version should move to 0.3.0 and the release notes must describe the governance assumptions.

docs.text:

  • Approve or amend the arbiter model (single arbiter vs two-key approval).
  • Confirm provider-level stake and opt-in-per-service.
  • Confirm the withdrawal precondition open_leases == 0 and the unbonding bound.
  • Confirm the error-code allocation (17–32) and event names before they become ABI.

docs.title: Design note: time-locked registry upgrades
docs.text: Status: draft for maintainer review. This note is required by CONTRIBUTING.md for a 200-point (high) issue. Implementation was requested explicitly, but merging the change is gated on a maintainer approving this design.

docs.title: 1. Problem
docs.text:
KeyLeaseRegistry::upgrade accepts a Wasm hash and calls deployer().update_current_contract_wasm in the same transaction. The admin can therefore replace the rules governing in-flight leases atomically with the upload, giving consumers no window to observe the change and revoke before new rules apply. Storage and balances survive an upgrade, which makes an exit window both useful and practical.

Impact: a compromised or hostile admin key can change settlement/refund logic without any warning period, defeating the consumer exit guarantee that the rest of the protocol is built around.

docs.title: 2. Invariants
docs.text:
1. No Wasm may be installed until a delay has elapsed since the proposal was recorded on-ledger.
  2. The admins who propose and execute may be the same key; the delay, not a second party, is the safety mechanism.
  3. There is always a cancel path, and cancellation never installs code.
  4. A proposal records the exact Wasm hash and the ledger timestamp after which it may execute, and both are readable by clients.
  5. Every state transition is authenticated by the current admin and emits a typed event; events never contain secret material.
  6. Upgrades keep the contract id, DataKey layout, stored values, token balances and in-flight leases. This change only adds an instance key.

docs.title: 3. Approach
docs.text:
• Add UPGRADE_DELAY_SECS = 86_400 (24 hours) as a public, documented constant, matching the existing settlement grace period.
  • Replace upgrade with three admin-only entry points:
  • propose_upgrade(admin, new_wasm_hash) — stores PendingUpgrade { new_wasm_hash, execute_after } under DataKey::PendingUpgrade (instance storage) and emits upgrade_proposed. A new proposal replaces a pending one and restarts the delay.
  • execute_upgrade(admin) — requires a pending proposal and ledger.timestamp() >= execute_after, installs the Wasm, clears the pending entry, and emits contract_upgraded with both the hash and the ledger timestamp. Executing early returns UpgradeDelayNotElapsed.
  • cancel_upgrade(admin) — clears the proposal and emits upgrade_cancelled.
  • Add get_pending_upgrade() -> Option<PendingUpgrade> as a read-only view.
  • Append error codes only (17, 18); never renumber existing codes.
  • Update the README interface/event tables and the deployment guide so operators use the new flow.

docs.title: Rejected alternatives
docs.text:
• Two-party approval / multisig — changes the trust model and needs a governance design outside this issue's scope.
  • Delay stored as a ledger sequence number — ledger timestamps are already how lease expiry works, and they make the delay human-readable (24h). A sequence number would couple the delay to close-time assumptions.
  • Keep the old instant upgrade for emergencies — that is exactly the unsafe path being removed; emergencies are covered by cancel_upgrade plus a fresh proposal.

docs.title: 4. Threat model
docs.text:
• Admin key compromise: the attacker can propose, but cannot install for at least 24 hours. Consumers can watch upgrade_proposed, use get_pending_upgrade, and revoke/settle before execute_after.
  • Front-running the execution: execute_upgrade re-checks the ledger timestamp at execution time; a proposal cannot be backdated.
  • Griefing by repeated proposals: an admin (or stolen key) can restart the clock, but this only ever delays an upgrade and never shortens the window.
  • Storage eviction: the pending entry lives in instance storage, whose TTL is extended to ~30 days by extend_instance_ttl; the 24-hour delay is well inside that horizon.
  • Event spoofing: events are published by the registry contract only, and the hash/ledger come from the stored proposal.

docs.title: 5. Test plan
docs.text:
• propose_upgrade stores the hash and execution ledger in the view and emits upgrade_proposed carrying both.
  • execute_upgrade before execute_after fails with UpgradeDelayNotElapsed and leaves the proposal intact.
  • cancel_upgrade removes the proposal and emits upgrade_cancelled; execution afterwards fails with NoPendingUpgrade.
  • Non-admins cannot propose, execute or cancel.
  • A proposal replaces a previous one and resets the clock.
  • Execution at/after the boundary installs the Wasm and publishes contract_upgraded with the hash and ledger. A 40-byte, hand-built module with a contractenvmetav0 metadata section is uploaded to the test host so the real update_current_contract_wasm primitive is exercised without a build-time Wasm dependency or third-party fixture.
  • Full CI gate: cargo fmt --all -- --check, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings, cargo test --all, and cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all.

docs.title: keylease-core v0.1.0
docs.text:
Superseded by v0.2.1. This page records the first release as it shipped; the current interface (events, upgrade, MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS) is in the contract reference.

First public release of the KeyLease registry contract.

KeyLease replaces long-lived static API/RPC credentials with time-bound, on-chain micro-leases: a consumer locks a micropayment in Soroban escrow and receives an authorization the provider can verify cheaply, with an automatic refund path if the provider goes offline.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Escrowed micro-leases. create_lease locks rate_per_call × requested_calls in a SEP-41 token and mints a lease that expires at ledger.timestamp() + duration_secs.
  • Provider settlement. settle_lease pays the provider for verified calls and refunds the remainder to the consumer. Settleable once the lease expires or once every allocated call is consumed.
  • Guaranteed consumer exit. revoke_expired_lease reclaims the full deposit 24 hours after expiry if the provider never settled — no support ticket required.
  • Service registry. Providers publish a rate and an endpoint_hash commitment instead of a secret, and can pause new leases.
  • Checked arithmetic throughout. Deposit and payout math aborts on overflow rather than truncating into a cheaper lease or a short refund.

docs.title: keylease-core v0.2.0
docs.text:
Soroban-native hardening: events, upgrades, storage-safe leases and re-entrancy protection.

This release moves the protocol closer to the Stellar primitives it depends on. The escrow model and the public lease lifecycle are unchanged, but the contract is now observable, upgradeable and hardened against hostile SEP-41 tokens.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Typed Soroban events. Every transition publishes a #[contractevent]: registry_initialized, escrow_token_set, service_registered, service_status_changed, lease_created, lease_settled, lease_revoked and contract_upgraded. Topics carry service_id / lease_id, so the lifecycle is indexable without polling storage.
  • On-chain metadata. contractmeta! embeds the name, version, description and repository in the Wasm, and version() returns the running version.
  • In-place upgrades. upgrade(admin, new_wasm_hash) installs a new Wasm through the Soroban deployer, preserving the contract id, storage and balances. Admin-only, and it emits contract_upgraded.
  • Checks-effects-interactions. settle_lease and revoke_expired_lease persist settled = true before calling the token. A new adversarial test installs a re-entrant token that calls back into settle_lease and asserts the second attempt is rejected.
  • TTL-safe lease durations. create_lease rejects durations above MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS (30 days) with the new DurationTooLong (16) error, and lease storage is extended for the term plus the 24h grace window. Escrow can no longer outlive its ledger entry.
  • Real SAC coverage. The suite now escrows through register_stellar_asset_contract_v2 — the same Stellar Asset Contract that wraps native XLM — in addition to the mock token.

docs.title: keylease-core v0.2.1
docs.text: Rent-aware lease storage. A Testnet deployment showed that extending every lease to the generic thirty-day horizon made Soroban storage rent dominate short leases: creating a 100-call, one-hour lease cost more in rent than the deposit itself. This release pays only for the storage time a lease can actually be used.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
• Lease TTL is term-aware. save_lease and get_lease extend a lease entry to (expires_at − now + 24h) / 5s + LEDGER_BUMP_THRESHOLD ledgers: the lease's remaining term, the provider's 24-hour grace window and a one-day read buffer.
  • No more month-long padding. A one-hour lease no longer rents thirty days of storage; the host still enforces its minimum persistent TTL (~7 days on Testnet), but the unnecessary padding is gone. A 30-day lease still gets the full term plus grace and buffer, under the network's maximum entry TTL.
  • Reads use the same policy. get_lease no longer bumps to a fixed thirty-day horizon, so a read near expiry does not silently pay a month of rent.
  • Verified on Testnet. CCEZYHUJ…TAFH62 runs this build; two leases were created, fully settled and partially settled on-chain. See Deployments.

docs.text:
